en: Preface to the Continued Commentary on the *Sūtra on the Method of Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*,
composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Chuxian. Regarding this sūtra,
our late patriarch, the Dhyāna Master Zhiyi, once took the perfect school (*yuanzong*) of Nāgārjuna as his foundation and attained a profound and wondrous realization.

According to the *Bianxuantong*, he had already composed commentaries and expositions that, in general, clarified the profound depths of the One Vehicle and elucidated the ultimate aim of the myriad practices.
However, during the final years of the Tang dynasty, these works were unfortunately subjected to the usual policy of incineration.

Consequently, those who carried their satchels of books fled to foreign lands, and thus the texts can no longer be found. Later, Master Gushan followed by producing his own work; however, its literary style and principles...
Scholars have long been troubled by its extreme brevity; therefore, my teacher Shenzhao has further composed a commentary (*yishu*).

Having reached only the initial stage, he was compelled to set down his pen due to urgent circumstances, so that the subsequent meanings remain unheard. Although I have spent many years at the Eastern Gate (the imperial academy) beneath the Wheel of Dharma, I have achieved nothing of value in my studies.
Thus, I feel deep pain that these subtle words are on the verge of falling into ruin, and I lament that previous efforts remain incomplete.

I, Yuan, have humbly emulated Zhiyi’s continuation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* and Daoxuan’s composition of the *Sengshi-lüe*, earnestly seeking spiritual assistance to complete this work in a fitting manner.
It has been divided into two volumes; may I also exert myself for the sake of our Way. Let readers not blame me for usurping the fame of others.
Commentary on the Meaning of the *Sūtra on the Method for Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Benru of Dongye;
continued and annotated by his disciple Chuxian.

The Great Dharma is vast and harmonious; it is taught without teaching, and its wondrous practice is realized through forgetting detachment, cultivated without cultivation. What was originally present is now absent;
this reveals the cause for realizing the true nature (*dharmatā*) that was previously recorded as the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

As the resonance between the capacity of beings and the response of the Buddha arises, question and answer reach perfect accord. Thus, the activities of the fixed *dharmadhātu* are established, and the perfect gate of Samantabhadra is opened. May [this merit] never... [end].

Alas, how great it is that those whose initial resolve lacks single-minded devotion to the signless (animitta) wish to realize the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and attain the *pratyāgama-dhāraṇī* in this very life, so that the seeds of the Dharma shall not be severed—is there any essential path other than this?

Although I am not clever, my aspiration lies in this sūtra; thus, following the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), I have hastily composed this commentary on its meaning, hoping thereby to fulfill my long-held vow.
I venture to say that this refers to the person [who embodies it].
First, in explaining the title, five meanings must be established: the "name" is the supreme and wondrous person and dharma; the "essence" is the opening of the provisional to reveal the true aspect;

the "principle" is the perfect contemplation of the One Vehicle; the "function" is the extinguishing of hindrances at the wondrous stage; and the "teaching" is the *amṛta* (nectar) of the *paramārtha*.
Since this is the concluding scripture of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, all five stages are wondrous. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"I now uphold this method of contemplating Samantabhadra Bodhisattva"—this is the Name (the teaching). "Single-mindedly contemplating the realm of the single reality" is the Substance (the essence).
"Not losing the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi" is the Principle (the purpose). How could one ever cease from this?
That the afflictions are purified and the various faculties are perfected is its function; that this Vaipulya Sūtra is the eye of all Buddhas is its teaching aspect.

The text of these five chapters is brilliantly clear. As for the profound purport of the five stages, which accords with the sequence of practice and possesses both beginning and end—who indeed is it but the Sage?
The *Buddhabhāṣita-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* has four parts for explaining its title:

first, the general and specific translations; second, the explanation of the title and its status; third, the word-by-word analysis; and fourth, the comprehensive interpretation according to the meaning. Regarding the general and specific:

the "Method of Practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" is the specific [title], while being collectively termed a "Sūtra" (*sūtra*) is the general [designation]. As for the establishment [of these terms]: "Samantabhadra" (Universal Worthy) refers to the specific, while "Method of Practice" (*caryā-dharma*) and "Sūtra" (*sūtra*) refer to the general. Thus, it is established.
This term "name" generally involves three meanings: first, in terms of teaching (*śāsana*), it refers to that which arises from conditions and from verbal expression;

second, in terms of practice (*caryā*), it refers to the subject that accords with and the object that is accorded to; third, in terms of principle (*tattva*), it refers to the name following the reality.

Thus, the two characters for "Buddha" represent the teaching, the character for "contemplation" (*guan*) represents the practice, and the meaning of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva corresponds to the principle. [The interlocutor] asked: "You have just said this is a 'name,' but now—"

If one asks, "What is the principle [li] here? the answer is: the meaning designated by a name is precisely the principle. For example, in the *Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guan wuliangshou jing*), that which is contemplated is the principle;

therefore, these three meanings are employed because they comprehensively encompass all dharmas, perfectly accord with the intent of the sūtra, and ensure that the teaching does not stand in isolation.
Furthermore, it is intended that practice shall not be erroneous or deviant, and that the principle shall differ from the partial and the Small Vehicle. This is the point. (2)
The Sanskrit name for the title is *Vairocana-mahābodhisattva*. *Vairocana* translates as "Universal Worthy" (*Puxian*).

The eight characters beginning with *mahā* translate as "Great Path-Mind Accomplishing Sentient Beings. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and this present sutra, he is named "Pien-chi" (Pervasive Auspiciousness).
He occupies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), and his name is honored by all who bow their heads in submission.
Because the Way is all-pervasive, it is called the "Universal Path" (*Puxian lun*); because the path is exhausted at the very limit of its final boundary, it is called the "Worthy Discourse.
Furthermore, it cites that the moon on the fourteenth night is like the moon on the fifteenth night—is this not what is meant?

Regarding the *Puxian lun*, the human and dharma aspects, essence and function, cause and effect, and original and trace aspects are as extensive as described in various texts (etc.). This is the third section: explaining the Buddha through characters.

"Buddha" (*buddha*) means "awakened," for he has fully awakened to the fact that all phenomena are wondrous. "Spoken" (*bhāṣita*) means "delighted," for it accords with his own original aspiration and the sentiments of sentient beings.

To distinguish this from the teachings of the four types of non-Buddhist teachers, it says "spoken by the Buddha. The Buddha possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as superior and inferior qualities;

the Dharma encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate. Here, the designation of the "speaker" is used broadly in its literal sense, yet specifically intended to refer to the [Buddha] who explains.
When Kāśyapa Muni moved from the inferior to the superior, sweeping away traces to reveal the fundamental, this was not even a recent occurrence at the site of tranquility (Śrāvastī);

how much less so at the Deer Park? Since the Master is thus, the Dharma he taught can be known. As for the observer, the observed, and the act of observing—these three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—and the awakened mind of the causal stage constitutes the totality of the practice gate.

Thus it is said: [The text continues with the verse: "The three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; The awakened mind of the causal stage is the totality of the practice gate. Thus it is.

Regarding the distinction between the sequential and the non-sequential, the *Sūtra of the Adornment of the Mahāyāna* (*Dazhuangyan jing*) states that the sequential contemplation consists of the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, also called the contemplation of the two truths;
and the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, also called the contemplation of equality.

By taking these two contemplations as skillful means, one enters the contemplation of the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein the mind and mental factors are quiescent, and one naturally flows [into liberation].

The vast differentiation of the essence and characteristics of the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is detailed as in other texts (*et cetera*). Regarding "one mind and three contemplations," the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, themselves provisionality, and themselves the Middle. Furthermore, the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states:
"The three wisdoms are truly attained within a single mind; it is but a single contemplation that, as three contemplations, contemplates the three truths, yet remains one."
Because they are the truths, this is called the "single mind and three contemplations. This contemplation is subtle and wondrous: one and three, three and one, one;
it contemplates all, all contemplate one, and one contemplates all. It is neither one nor all. What practice of contemplation is there that is not subsumed within such a contemplation?
The meaning of the character "contemplation" (guan) in the title lies precisely here. Thus, the Sutra says: "Not dwelling in the ocean of afflictions..."

To sever the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such that these characteristics of phenomena neither arise nor perish, but remain seated in mindfulness of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), is precisely this meaning.
Furthermore, because this contemplating subject must eliminate the conceptualization of self-nature, it is said: "Neither internal nor external observation;
one attains Bodhi therein. It is neither identical to nor separate from this wondrous state. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is the object of contemplation.

Furthermore, the principle-treasury of the Dharma-realm is non-different yet differentiated, and thus the three bodies are taught: the white jade and purple gold [bodies] correspond to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body);
the boundless sounds correspond to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body); and the body being like space corresponds to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
Being different yet non-different, this is Vairocana pervading all places. Taking this as the object, what dharma would not be harmonized? Moreover, it is also...
This practitioner’s mind is the essence of mind; because the mind acts as the mind, the Sūtra says:

"There is no suchness outside of wisdom that can be realized, nor is there a suchness outside of wisdom that serves as the object entered by wisdom. Only when the mind is free from all dependencies is it called the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).
"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to advancing toward [the goal], while "dharma" (*dharma*) refers to the rules and norms. This present Sūtra is the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.

While other sutras contain extensive categories of meaning (*arthamukha*), this text specifically clarifies a single intent. Regarding the term "sutra" (*sūtra*): it is defined as "dharma" and "constant.

Originating from the golden mouth of the Sage, its names may be translated or not translated, and their meanings encompass many aspects. As fully detailed in the *Mysterious Text on the Lotus Sutra*, there are four ways to harmonize these meanings through their principles:
"contemplation" (*guan*) refers to the practice of contemplative illumination (*guan-chaogui*), while "Universal Worthy" (*Samantabhadra*) refers to the practice of true nature (*zhenxinggui*).
The practice of the Dharma is the primary section on the "Aids to Accomplishment" (*sādhana*); since the title is thus integrated, the intent of the Sūtra becomes clear.
Furthermore, it may be harmonized with all threefold dharmas (and so forth). Therefore, the Sūtra text states that if one hears even the name of this title, the merit is immeasurable (and so forth).
Next, regarding the identification of the essence (*tattva*): the essence is the fundamental substance, the deep reservoir of the entire Sūtra and the locus of its manifold meanings.

The ultimate aim of all schools of practice and the fundamental basis for the arising of the teachings are like the myriad stars revolving around the North Star, or like the ten thousand streams flowing toward the Eastern Sea.
The ancient masters pointed to the causes as being the true reality (*dharmatā*); thus, they identified the school (*zong*) with the essence (*ti*), rather than treating them as distinct.

Recent scholars have erred by failing to clarify this simplicity, making it difficult to perceive the wondrous essence. Now, by opening up the provisional to reveal the true reality, [the essence is made manifest].
The true realm constitutes the essential body of the Sūtra, while all else is the work of Māra.

If distinguished according to the person, it takes up the meaning of the single point of the *dharmakāya*, as is commonly explained. Furthermore, its essence contains the three virtues (*triguṇa*): namely, *līḍi*, *da*, and *lī*. "Lī" signifies the supreme honor of a sovereign or father;
"ḍi" signifies the ultimate depth and profundity; and "da" signifies pervading the boundaries without limit. These three are one.

By clarifying their mutual relationship, they are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they parallel or separate; through the distinction between "one" and "three," the roles of subject and object are clearly defined.
To facilitate easy understanding, a general title is established to represent their names. To speak of them specifically:

the Dharma-body of Samantabhadra encompasses all phenomena, being neither vertical nor horizontal, and neither cause nor effect—this constitutes its essence. Furthermore, the dharmas of practice are likewise not vertical.
Not being partial, it serves as the perfect cause that encompasses all phenomena to fulfill their respective functions. As the sutra says:
"This is the Great Dharma Seal, the ocean of Parinirvāṇa, which can give birth to the three kinds of pure Buddha-bodies.

A practitioner should realize that the one mind and all phenomena are free from the four types of slander and transcend the hundred negations; only then can they be said to have wondrously attained the essence of the sutra. (3)

One who clarifies the fundamental principle (zong) does not see difference as distinct from non-difference; this is the pivot for manifesting the essence (ti), the vital gateway for practice, and the governing framework for attaining the fruit.
The categories of the essence likewise comprise three meanings: the fundamental principle (zongben), the essential principle (zongyao), and the auxiliary principle (zongzhu).

These correspond to the entirety of reality giving rise to contemplation—neither identical nor different—just as a single golden substance forms various vessels, or as the face of heaven appears in diverse reflections.

The Three Eyes now insistently follow the essential meaning: that which is the contemplation of the One Vehicle mind (*ekayāna-citta*) as being neither essence nor function, yet serving as both cause and fruit, constitutes the core tenet of this school.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "You should now contemplate the Mahāyāna cause;

it should be known that the Mahāyāna cause is the reality-correspondence (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. The single character "contemplation" (*guan*) in the title refers to the perfection of the three kinds of *prajñā*.

The ultimate purport of the Sudden school (*dun-zong*) is the function of the fourfold discernment (*si-bian*), wherein the subtle point lies in the extinction of hindrances; this is the power of the present sutra.

It is like piercing a drum with a mallet or striking the earth with a hoe, or like ascending into the void and seeing objects. The examples of the school (*zong*) also comprise three meanings: the fundamental function (*ben-yong*), the situational function (*dang-yong*), and the autonomous function (*zi-zai-yong*).
Taking the entirety of principle as function, it is neither one nor many, analogous to the single substance of a mirror and its images, or the character "yi" (伊).
Regarding the three dots of the character [for "emptiness"] in the present sutra’s intent: because evil causes have not been eliminated, the wondrous realm remains obscured.

Therefore, the text specifically clarifies repentance; though undivided, it is divided for the sake of exposition. It is neither the primary principle nor the essence, but takes the three gates of liberation as its function.
Thus the sutra says: "The merit of this contemplation removes all obstacles, allowing one to see the supreme, wondrous forms. By means of this superior function, it adorns [the practitioner].
When the profound and wondrous wisdom is perfected and the body of reality is manifested, the great fruit is fully realized; it is here that the merit of practicing the Dharma resides.

If one understands the three liberations, then the meaning of repentance—the Vow of Samantabhadra’s Practices and Vows, which leaves nothing outside of a single moment—is such that it can be accomplished even at the initial stage of the mind.
As for the "Phases of the Five Teachings," this constitutes the fifth part, the supreme nectar of ghee.
Furthermore, the meaning elucidated in the Four Teachings is the revelation that the Perfect is identical to each of the teachings, and each teaching is identical to the Perfect;
it is neither one nor many, and is inconceivable. This is the "speech according to one's own intent," for it is the realm of the Buddhas.
Thus, a sutra says: "This is the Buddha-eye, which gives birth to the lineage of all Tathāgatas. Regarding the [Lotus] Section, this wondrous necessity must be understood.
Since this is the main section that concludes the sutra, there is no other path; the fivefold contemplation of the mind is as explained in the *Xuanwen* (and so forth).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kaśmīr during the Liu Song dynasty.
This sutra was translated by the Kasmirian śramaṇa Dharmamitra—whose name means "Dharma-Excellence" (Fashou)—during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
He arrived in Jianye at the age of Jiazi and translated it at Zhihuan Temple. Although it has been transmitted and practiced for many years, its continuity has lacked proper care;
thus, I hope to fulfill my aspiration to propagate it and look up to repay the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs by printing and distributing it.
The preface to this scripture in ten thousand scrolls by the Indian Master Ciyun is already detailed.

Beginning on the Mid-Autumn Festival of the *renwu* year of the Qingli era of the Great Song dynasty, I exhausted my foolish efforts in lecturing and instruction, expounding the scripture day after day and composing a commentary (*shu*) word by word.

By following the finger to see the moon, I have sought to aid the enlightenment of those in their final studies; yet, having obtained the rabbit and discarded the snare, how could I possibly hope to merit the gaze of one of profound insight?
However, consciousness can express this Dharma-body; the life of wisdom transcends liberation precisely through these very characters.
How could it not be by means of this? The explanation of the title is thus concluded.
△ Next, the explanation of the scriptural text is divided into three parts: first, from "Thus" up to "external matters of the various obstacles" constitutes the introduction. Second...

From "The Buddha told Ānanda, 'Listen attentively'" down to the end of the verses constitutes the *zhengzong* (the main body of the teaching). From the conclusion of these three verses down to the end of the sutra constitutes the *liutongxu* (the introductory section for circulation).
Generally, there are three types of such introductions: first, the sequential introduction (*cixiuyushi*), which describes the sequence of events;

second, the general introduction (*tongxiuyushi*), as all sutras alike possess a sequential order; and third, the specific introduction (*biexiuyushi*), which differs from one sutra to another. This is because while the general name [of the sutra] exists, [the specific circumstances] vary.

Regarding the general introduction and the specific title, there is a separate introduction (and so forth). In this present sutra, the initial five points constitute the sequence for establishing faith and understanding (*śraddhā-prasāda*).
The scripture states: "I announce to all bhikṣus: I shall now enter parinirvāṇa. This constitutes the specific introduction (*pratyeka-nidāna*), which serves as the causal basis;
it simply lacks a detailed narrative account.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Vaiśālī, in the multi-storied lecture hall of the Great Forest Monastery (Mahāvana-vihāra).

Now, this is explained in two parts: first, the general explanation, and second, the specific explanation. Regarding the general explanation: "Thus" refers to the beginning of faith; "I heard" means personally receiving the words of the teaching;
"at one time" indicates the moment of the response between teacher and disciple; and "Buddha" specifically identifies the Lord of Transformation.

The lecture hall is the place for hearing the sutras; all such things are intended to encourage and bring to completion the future generation’s joyful seeing and hearing, so that they may give rise to goodness, cease doubt, and achieve the Way.
Next, regarding the separate explanation of "thus" (*tathā*): in other sutra texts, it means "according to principle," "not different," or "not otherwise.
This interpretation applies universally to the present statement as well; within the "Marvelous" (*miao*), the absence of marks (*animitta*) is what is meant by "as described."

Chun-shih said: "To examine this transmission in detail, how could this possibly be the same as others? It is all the more trustworthy; therefore it says, 'Thus. One who observes and understands in this way is called 'in accordance with principle' (如理).
To be free from discursive thought is called 'the mind like the mind' (如心). Not seeing the mind is called 'is. Thus the Sūtra says: 'The mind is purely Dharma;
it is in accord with Dharma. This is it. As for 'I have heard,' this is spoken according to worldly convention; it refers to the harmony of the 'self' (我) and its conditions."

To "proclaim" and "hear" means that outwardly it does not deviate from what is appropriate, and inwardly it does not contradict reality. Thus, the three teachings all refer to the faculties and objects as "I hear.
For the person of the Perfect Teaching, the self is precisely hearing; because color (form) is the true self, it is called "self.

Since there is no hearing apart from nature, and no nature apart from hearing, and since even non-nature is non-existent, it is called "hearing. One who contemplates and understands should reflect back upon this hearing.
The nature of the mind is empty, the self is empty, and hearing is also empty; being without hearing and without attainment, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Therefore it is said, "My own mind is itself empty," and again, "When the practitioner has heard this, their mind is not startled or terrified.
This "at once" refers to the moment of resonance with the Middle Way. Whether [the dharmas] are long or short, provisional or real, is not discussed here. Within this—
"One time" (*ekakāla*) refers to the inconceivable *dharmatā* entering all times as one time.

As the *Ekakṣaṇābhisambodha-sūtra* states: "Sixty minor *kalpas* are said to be like the duration of a meal. For the practitioner who contemplates and understands, the object and the contemplation are identical (*yuganaddha*), and subject and object are both extinguished;
this is called "one sudden, wondrous realization" (*ekahakkhara-miyo-kei*). Being transparently clear like space, it is called "time. As the *Sūtra on Contemplation* states: "Contemplate..."

The mind is without mental phenomena and does not abide in dharmas; it is also said that one enters the Bodhisattva’s stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) immediately upon the opportune moment.

"Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Qin (Chinese), it means "the Awakened One. This refers to one who has fully awakened to the three periods of time, to sentient beings, and to all worldly and world-transcending categories—both the enumerated and the non-enumerated, the permanent and the impermanent—and having attained complete and thorough great enlightenment, is thus called a Buddha. Since the three types of awakening are perfected, the ten titles are fully possessed.

When words are truthful, what is heard may be trusted. Now, by defining the meaning of the *dharmakāya* through the perspective of the *sarvākārajñatā*, this constitutes one of the three [bodies] and is forever distinct from previous explanations;
only thus does this scripture reveal its capacity to teach. As for the contemplative understanding of the Teacher who expounds it:

because the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) suddenly realizes that the phenomena of the mind are of a single mark, which is markless, and even that marklessness is absent—therefore, it is called "contemplation" (*cintā*).
The meaning of the Dharma as true quiescence is free from all marks of conceptual discrimination; this is precisely what is meant by "recalling the Buddha’s body of great awakening.

"In Vaiśālī" refers to the location where the sutra was preached, the wondrous place of reliance. By citing the location, he encourages faith, showing that the preaching of the sutra has a specific setting.
Many other sutras also frequently state "residing in" (*viharati*), which means "dwelling. In the treatise, there are generally four ways of explaining the meaning of "dwelling."
The meaning is this: if those who dwell—such as devas, Brahmās, sages, or Buddhas—are distinct, then the realms in which they dwell must likewise differ accordingly.
Now, when it says "the Buddha’s dwelling," it refers to the Śūraṅgama; by citing the supreme, all that is inferior is necessarily included. Vaiśālī means "Extensive and Pure";
because its territory is broad and level, it is called the City of Extensiveness, and because its moats and ramparts are magnificent and beautiful, it is so named.
The "Dharma-gate of Adornment and Purity" refers to the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni, which is fundamentally abiding in the eternally quiescent Dharma-realm;
its boundless nature is vast and expansive, adorned by the excellence of goodness and free from all defilement and evil—this is called "Adornment and Purity.

Although its traces reside in the human world within the country of Vaipulya, this name, though borrowed from conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), actually signifies the realm in which it dwells. As for the contemplation of the mind:

Contemplating this mind-nature as being like empty space, endowed with two kinds of adornment, undefiled and unattached, and ultimately pure, it is said that it "constantly dwells in the city of Nirvana.
When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; it is not something separate.

Regarding "the great forest" and so forth, these specifically indicate the location where the sutra was preached. A dense thicket with many trunks and branches is called a "great grove," where various trees grow intertwined and lean upon one another.

It is said that the "forest" (vana) refers to the pure abode of people; its essence can serve as a place for rest, hence it is called a "dwelling" (layana). The perilous eaves layered one upon another are termed a "multi-storied pavilion" (kūṭāgāra), which is a place of peace and liberation.
That which is called the "lecture hall" (śālā) is the Dharma-gate, for the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) encompasses all without exception.

That which is called the "great forest" is because it is fully endowed with myriad virtues. Being free from inversion is the essence; the emptiness of the aggregates (skandha-śūnyatā) is the dwelling, the multi-storied pavilion.
Thus, the Hall of the Samādhi of the Profound Emptiness is the Great Capital of the Dharma-realm; the method for contemplating the mind can be understood by analogy with what was stated above (etc.).

Those not included among the assembly of fellow listeners in the sutras have been omitted here. Are the ten thousand devaputras and the various great bodhisattvas at the end of the sutra not these very individuals?

△ Next, regarding the specific introductory section: as various sutras differ—some describing the Buddha’s initial silence and stillness after his awakening, some featuring the golden mouth proclaiming names without being questioned, some using the guise of evil and rebellion to expound pure karma, or relying on demonic illusions to discuss secret samādhis—this sutra proclaims *nirvāṇa* to cause sentient beings to yearn for it, thereby serving as its introduction.
The text is divided into two parts; first, as follows:
The two Great Beings arose and requested that he announce his passing;
he then informed the bhikṣus, "In three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
His initial announcement to the bhikṣus regarding the three months refers to the month of Jizi (the eleventh lunar month) if following the summer retreat schedule.
Having announced this to the assembly on the day of the full moon, the three months were completed on the fifteenth day of the second month.
The day the month was fulfilled symbolizes the Dharma of perfect luminosity upon the Middle Way. "Constant" is itself "impermanent," and "impermanent" is itself "constant.

As for "I," once the fruit of Great Enlightenment is realized, the sense of a sovereign self is forgotten; now, according to the conventional usage of the Dharma King who has shattered existence and possesses the eight masteries, [he speaks thus].
This designation was established because it accords with what is appropriate. "Parinirvāṇa" is fully called *mahā-parinirvāṇa*, which is translated here as "Great Quiescent Extinction.
However, Nirvana is fundamentally beyond names and designations, and is not within the reach of form or emptiness.
That it is now employed to address the assembly is because, through the maturation of the perfect capacity and the skillful means of great compassion, the fan is raised and moved.

By planting trees, one attains both seeing and hearing; this collectively cites three causes and three points to designate them as "Great Nirvana," intended to gladden and encourage those who are ready for the teaching, thereby bringing about the realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
As it says: "Those who should be delivered by means of extinction (nirvāṇa) are shown to attain extinction"—this is precisely its meaning.
△ Next, the Great Being’s Request consists of two parts: first, the description of the reverent demeanor of the three sages; second, the formal posing of the questions.
Venerable Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in *añjali*, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and prostrated before him.
Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he joined his palms and gazed intently at the Tathāgata, not for a moment averting his eyes. Elder Mahākāśyapa... [text continues]
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya also rose from his seat, joined his palms in homage, and gazed up at the Honored Countenance.

As for the respectful demeanor [of Ānanda], because he is worthy of veneration by all ordinary practitioners, he is called the Venerable (Bhadanta). Ānanda is translated here as "Joyful Celebration" (Qingxi);
he was the younger cousin of the Tathāgata. He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, and the entire kingdom celebrated with great joy.

It is for this reason that he is so named. His rising from his seat is likewise like the ritual of Confucian disciples in this land who rise when requesting further instruction or inquiry from their master;
thus he rises to manifest his constant contemplation of the ultimate principle.

Because his wisdom of non-abiding does not dwell in compassion, yet his compassion of abiding-in-existence is ever-present, it is said that he rises from his seat, adjusts his robes, and joins his palms to manifest [this truth].

With the wondrous understanding of non-duality, he circumambulated the Buddha three times to signify that his perfect capacity was about to be awakened. Regarding the phrase "contemplating with equanimity" and so forth:
having heard the Buddha’s proclamation of his passing into extinction, he harbored deep longing within; desiring to present his petition, he gazed upward from without.
He contemplated the true reality of his own body, and his contemplation of the Buddha was likewise so. Śākyamuni is named Vairocana; this very body of mine is [that very same].
Because this is the Dharma-body, it is called "Truth" (*satya*). Furthermore, as for "contemplating truth," it refers to the wondrous compassion that is without conditions (*anālambana-maitrī*);
by appealing to the Great Sage, it brings enlightenment to all beings. Thus, it is said that "compassion does not take sentient beings as its object, nor does it take phenomena as its object;
it takes the Tathāgata as its object. Therefore, it is called "without conditions. Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Venerable Drinker of Light"—was an ancient seer (*ṛṣi*).

The distant descendants of humanity were named after him; Maitreya is translated here as "The Benevolent One" (Cishi), for he gathers in sentient beings through unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*).
The three sages share the same appearance to symbolize the single path. Thus it is said:
"When asked about the time of his parinirvāṇa, why do only these three sages arise to answer? Ānanda was the Buddha’s attendant and was about to compile the Dharma.
Because he preserved [the Dharma], Kāśyapa received the entrustment to be the first patriarch after the extinction;

because Maitreya shall succeed him as the next Buddha, the responsibility they bear is exceedingly grave, and thus they have raised their voices in unison to inspire [the assembly]. Furthermore, the three sages represent the three virtues:
Ānanda represents *prajñā* (wisdom), Kāśyapa represents *vimukti* (liberation), and Maitreya represents the *dharmakāya*. These are three yet one, termed the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
That the merit of practicing transformation for others returns to this—how could it be in vain?
△ Second, the formal posing of the question:
At that time, the three Great Beings, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, how..."
When sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta and practice the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, they should contemplate with right mindfulness the realm of the single reality (*eka-yāna*).
How can they not lose the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment?

Furthermore, how may they continue to harbor afflictions (*kleśa*) and remain amidst the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) while purifying their faculties, extinguishing all transgressions, and attaining the pure, eternal eye born of one's parents?
Without severing the five desires, one is able to perceive all external objects that constitute hindrances.

Regarding the phrase "different mouths" and so forth: it is intended to open the wondrous gate of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). It prefigures the ritual posture of the mouth, wherein the three are fused and merged into the one;
thus it is said "different mouths," and since the three are identical to the one, it is called "unified voice. In the formal inquiry, [the text] proceeds from the Tathāgata.
After the extinction [of the Buddha], one seeks instruction on the single reality realm (*eka-tattva-gocara*) regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta and its practice;

this constitutes a comprehensive inquiry into the name, essence, and purpose—the third [section]. The Vaipulya sūtras constitute the inquiry into the name. Right mindfulness and reflection constitute the inquiry into the purpose.

The single reality realm constitutes the inquiry into the essence. "Vaipulya" refers to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which elucidates the principle; it is not the third [turning of the wheel].

At that time, entering the cool pond through the four gates, it is said that the principle accorded with in each location is uniform; thus they are called "equal. To ask separately, "How is it that one does not lose this equality?
is the specific inquiry regarding the core tenet. The Buddha’s fruit is perfectly penetrating and is described as supreme;

because merit returns to that which is able to accord with it, it points to the initial thought-moment and so forth. To further clarify this is what is meant by "not losing" it. How, moreover, should one proceed?
Downward, it extends to all external matters that constitute obstacles; these are intended for specific inquiry and application.

As for "not severing and not departing from the pure faculties to extinguish transgressions," this means to suddenly forget all obstructions and wondrously accord with the perfect and eternal. The function of the Great Repentance lies precisely here.

Regarding the phrase "the pure and constant eye," the intent encompasses all six sense faculties; however, for the time being, we shall follow the initial sequence and take the eye as the starting point.

Question: The Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*) is fundamentally an exposition of the title; yet now it is used to judge the entire scripture. This has not been heard of since antiquity. Answer:

The title is general while the scripture is specific; how could there be different paths? Although other scriptures have [fivefold meanings], they are simply not like the sequence of question and answer found in this scripture.
If you say that it cannot be used to judge the scripture, then how can you claim that every chapter within it fully possesses [this meaning]?

Beneath each sentence concerning the "essence" (*tǐ*) and so forth, the sublime name (*mìomíng*) is invariably appended. Now, this sutra discusses practice, which is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*; it is appropriate to judge the five meanings of the sutra according to the ten stages of the vehicle (*shíshèng*). This does not mean that the five meanings are the answer to the ten stages; rather, the ten stages are roughly identical in their general outline. However, while the five meanings provide the opening of understanding (*kāijiě*), the ten stages establish practice (*lìxíng*); thus, there is a slight difference between understanding and practice. If one seeks to harmonize them so they are identical: [The five meanings correspond to the ten stages as follows: 1. The meaning of the title (*míngyì*) corresponds to the first stage, the stage of the true cause (*zhēnyīn shèng*). 2. The meaning of the essence (*tǐyì*) corresponds to the second stage, the stage of the true effect (*zhēnguǒ shèng*). 3.

The meaning of the characteristics (*xiàngyì*) corresponds to the third stage, the stage of the true function (*zhēnyòng shèng*). 4. The meaning of the power (*língyì*) corresponds to the fourth stage, the stage of the true penetration (*zhēntōng shèng*). 5. The meaning of the teaching (*jiàoyì*) corresponds to the fifth stage, the stage of the true entry (*zhènruò shèng*). 6. The meaning of the person (*rényì*) corresponds to the sixth stage, the stage of the true position (*zhènwèi shèng*). 7. The meaning of the method (*fǎyì*) corresponds to the seventh stage, the stage of the true practice (*zhēnxíng shèng*). 8. The meaning of the sequence (*cìdì yì*) corresponds to the eighth stage, the stage of the true sequence (*zhèncì shèng*). 9.

The meaning of the response (*huìyì*) corresponds to the ninth stage, the stage of the true correspondence (*zhènfú shèng*). 10. The meaning of the benefit (*lìyì*) corresponds to the tenth stage, the stage of the true benefit (*zhènlì shèng*). Thus, the five meanings and the ten stages are fundamentally one and the same. It is simply that the former elucidates the principles of understanding, while the latter establishes the framework for practice; the distinction lies merely in the relative emphasis on understanding versus practice. If one brings them together, they are made identical.

Although they are not distinct, the differentiation of the ten vehicles serves to manifest the principle of the essence; once the principle is established, the function of the sūtra is to destroy delusion, and once delusion is destroyed, the essence of the sūtra is revealed.
These five meanings encompass all dharmas, and the ten vehicles are likewise so.
What would be improper about using the ten vehicles to explain the sūtra? However, for the purposes of the question and answer in this current text, the five meanings are more convenient.
△ Second, the main body of the text is divided into two parts: first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka). The prose section is further divided into two:

first, a brief response, and second, an extensive response. Within the brief response, there are two sections: first, the admonition and permission, and second, the actual response. Within the permission, there are two parts:
first, identifying the past and pointing to the present, and second, granting permission to speak briefly and extensively.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
In the past, at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and other dwelling places, the Tathāgata has already extensively analyzed the Way of Single Reality.
Now, at this place, he does so for the sake of all sentient beings of future ages who wish to practice the unsurpassed Dharma of the Mahāyāna and who wish to study the conduct of Samantabhadra."
Regarding the first admonition: because the path is received through the faculty of the ear, the Buddha-dharma must first admonish one to listen attentively.

From this, the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) arises; from this, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises well; and from mindfulness, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises.

When these three wisdoms are perfected—like a vessel that is turned upward and intact—one can receive the water of the Dharma. Thus it is said: "By means of hearing, the person who practices through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) [attains realization]."
Therefore, there is wisdom that arises from wisdom, and the practitioner of the path attains concentration through reflection, which in turn gives rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
One should know that although this land possesses two faculties, it follows the practice of faith because its faculty is strong; thus, he now exhorts them to listen.
"Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain" is the designation for the location where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached in the past, as well as other places where he resided.
Since this location is where the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached, it is called the "One Reality. Now, regarding the reference below:

although this is currently the Vaiśālī Vihāra, it is primarily intended for future generations. The Mahāyāna Dharma is the objective realm upon which one relies, while the practices of Samantabhadra are the conduct to be practiced.
One who studies these practices travels from the sea of birth and death to the shore of Nirvāṇa, and thereafter [the teaching] will spread widely.
To transform sentient beings and bring the Buddha-dharma to fulfillment is like Pūrṇa seeking to study Prajñāpāramitā;

because he wishes to enter the Middle Way correctly from the two extremes, and because he wishes to practice the Mahāyāna, this is a general reference to the Perfect Gate (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). To study Samantabhadra is a specific application to the present teaching.
Briefly listed here are these two categories according to their respective inclinations and desires.
△ Next, I shall permit a brief explanation of what has been extensively taught.
I will now explain the method of recollection: whether one sees Samantabhadra or does not see him, all accumulated offenses shall be eliminated.
I shall now provide a detailed analysis for you all, Ānanda: the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra was born in the Pure and Wondrous Land of the East.
The characteristics of that land have already been explained in detail within the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra*.
Regarding the recollection of the Dharma, this passage sets forth its essential tenets; as for whether it is seen or not seen, this briefly indicates its substance;

and regarding the elimination of the count of transgressions, this briefly brings out its function. The Bodhisattva questioned [the Buddha] based on these three meanings, and the Tathāgata answered him.
Through these three meanings, the principle is made clear. In the brief explanation, the mention of the East refers to the land upon which the Lord of this Dharma-gate relies.

Samantabhadra arises from his own essence, the serene light (*śāntaprabhā*), and manifests a response in the same realm as the Eastern direction—the beginning of the quarters and the first of the stages.
From the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the Bodhisattva constantly responds to the Dharma.

The principle of the beginning and end of the realms is one and the same; furthermore, it reveals the perfect capacity. Initial practice arises in reliance upon this principle, giving rise to the three kinds of bodies.

The initial mind is difficult [to realize], and by means of this, [the practitioner] manifests [the truth] by entrusting it to the primary retribution body (*sambhogakāya*). This is the object of contemplation in the present.

Having extensively clarified the characteristics of the lands, he then points to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Question: How should one broadly differentiate and briefly explain this? Answer: For the practitioner...
The meaning of purifying the six sense faculties through the repentance of transgressions is extensive when treated broadly, as in the manifestation of Samantabhadra;
it is concise when treated briefly, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Although this is called a brief exposition, within this very scripture, it is precisely answered in detail.
△ Second, within the detailed response, there are two parts: first, a general presentation of the object and the contemplation; second, a specific presentation of the modes of practice.
Within the general presentation, the first is the identification of the person, which answers the previous [point] on not losing bodhicitta and anticipates the core of the inquiry.
I shall now briefly explain this for you, Ānanda: if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
or any sentient beings among the eight classes of gods, nāgas, and others, who recite Mahāyāna sūtras, practice the Mahāyāna path, have resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna,
or who long to behold the physical body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva or the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
Those who wish to see Śākyamuni Buddha and his manifested Buddhas, those who wish to attain the purity of the six sense faculties, should study this contemplation.
The merit of this contemplation removes all obstacles; one sees supreme and wondrous forms even without entering *samādhi*, simply by reciting and upholding it.
By practicing with single-minded devotion, with each thought following the next without departing from the Mahāyāna, for even a single day...
Those who encounter heavy obstacles will see Samantabhadra after twenty-one days; those with even heavier obstacles will see him after forty-nine days;

others with heavier obstacles will see him within one lifetime; others with heavier obstacles will see him within two lifetimes; and others with the heaviest obstacles will see him within three lifetimes.
Because such karmic retributions differ in these various ways, there are these diverse explanations.

The Sūtra mentions the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings in order to clarify the fundamental principle (*mūla*) that enables realization; first, it indicates the capacities (*adhikāra*) for practicing that principle.
Those who recite the Mahāyāna possess the understanding for practicing the principle; those who practice the Mahāyāna represent the beginning of practicing the principle;
and those who resolve upon the Mahāyāna represent the goal of practicing the principle. When these three matters are without deficiency, the wondrous principle is established. I desire—

Seeing the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, one attains the purification of the faculties; since there is nothing that does not take wisdom as its foundation, the text concludes by stating, "One should practice this contemplation.

These three subsequent phrases answer the question regarding how the purification of the faculties is attained, demonstrating their function in generating wholesome qualities while removing all obstacles.
This reveals the power of manifestation in producing goodness, and seeing the sublime forms above clarifies the function of destroying [afflictions].
The virtue of those with evil [karma] does not enter samādhi; however, for those who merely recite and uphold [the text], they will achieve the completion of practice through these causes.

Although Mount Nanyue spoke of the "practice of peaceful bliss with signs" (*sanimitta-śukhavihāra*) and the "practice of peaceful bliss without signs" (*animitta-śukhavihāra*), these names were established based on specific conditions and do not represent a fundamental difference.

Although this current text specifically indicates that reciting the sutras and repenting of transgressions serve as gateways for awakening and entry, it does not mean that [these practices alone constitute the entirety].
Because it is an inconceivable contemplation, it is said that one should cultivate it with single-minded devotion.

As for the differences in the number of days and years in the present and future lives, these pertain to the practitioner themselves. This is because karmic obstructions vary in thickness, the application of the mind varies in stillness or distraction, and the methods of contemplation vary in clarity or obscurity;
therefore, it is so. Furthermore, according to this sutra, [the results] extend far back to three lifetimes. As for the Avataṃsaka Sūtra...
After further passing through kalpas, one may finally behold it.

△ Second, the correct demonstration of the characteristics of practice: from "From the body-measure of Samantabhadra" down to "the realm of the single reality" is the extensive answer concerning the essence of the inquiry regarding the arousal of the mind and its cultivation;
from "At that time, the practitioner, having seen these things" down to the end [of the section] is the conclusion.
This clearly and extensively answers the question regarding not losing the intent of Bodhi;

having already seen the Buddhas of the ten directions and the elephant atop one’s head in a dream, the prose section extensively answers the question regarding the application of attaining the purification of the faculties.

The treasury of the three virtues is used daily by sentient beings, yet they do not know it; the Sage has separately composed the explanations on the essence (*tattva*) and so forth, in order to cause them to realize it.
The Dharma-realm sentient beings rely upon the essence to cultivate the school, repenting their transgressions to achieve the realization of the Human Secret Treasury (*puruṣa-guhya-kośa*).
How great indeed is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Great Sage! This initial section has two parts: first, revealing the essence by way of the sacred realm;

second, clarifying that wondrous practice is able to manifest it. The first part also has two sections: first, entering the kingdom through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); second, transforming the elephant through the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*).
The entry into the country by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) illustrates the essence [of reality] by way of its objective sphere.

Although the body, voice, and physical form of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva are boundless, he employs his sovereign supernormal power to contract his body into a small size when intending to come to this country; this is because the obstructions of the people of Jambudvīpa are heavy.

Because the principle and phenomena of this retribution are vast and extensive, it is called "boundless. It is quiescently illuminating and perfectly interfused, responding to conditions without deliberation.
Because the capacities [of sentient beings] are inferior, the Sage manifests inferiority and conceals his true reality to establish provisional means; thus it is said that he "shortens his body.
However, this is merely what is perceived by those whose karmic obstructions are heavy.
△ Thus, by the power of wisdom, he transforms himself into an elephant to manifest his essence.
By the power of wisdom, he manifests as one riding a white elephant; this elephant has six tusks and seven limbs that touch the ground. Beneath each of these seven limbs grow seven *māyūrī* flowers.
The color of the elephant is a brilliant white, such that even the finest white things—such as crystal or the Snow Mountains—cannot compare to it.
The body of this elephant is four hundred and fifty yojanas long and four hundred yojanas high. At the tips of its six tusks are six bathing pools;
in each pool grow fourteen lotus flowers equal in size to the pools themselves.
When these flowers bloom, they are like the king of celestial trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*). Upon each flower sits a jade maiden whose complexion is radiant and surpasses that of the celestial maidens.
From his hands, five *kōng hóu* lutes spontaneously manifested;
each lute had five hundred musical instruments as its retinue, and there were five hundred birds—ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks—all of jewel-like color, born amidst the flowers and leaves.
From the elephant’s trunk emerged flowers whose stalks were like the color of red pearls, their petals golden, still closed and unopened.

The wondrous wisdom attained by the wise Samantabhadra, the perfect teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding its original and manifested traces, and the numinous source of the Dharma-realm—these are the mothers of all Buddhas.
That they manifest as a white elephant is a case of sudden existence from non-existence; it is the transformation of what was originally non-existent into present existence.
Thus, the brilliant whiteness of its color signifies that the essence of wisdom is in profound accord with principle; it is the very substance of the Dharmakāya.
Originally free from black or evil, it is able to bear the burden of all beings through the power of compassion; thus it is called the "White Elephant.
Its length of four hundred and fifty *yojanas* signifies that the ultimate place of treasure is reached by only one person, the Buddha, and thus completes the five hundred.
Since this is the realm of the *Samyaksambuddha*, it is reduced by fifty. Its height of four hundred signifies that Samantabhadra dwells in the four stages.

Because it is above all else, it is called "high. Its six tusks symbolize the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); the ponds at the tips of the tusks represent the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
These eight liberations are the essence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), while the six supernormal powers are its functional application; thus, essence and function are mutually identical.

Within the ponds there are fourteen lotus flowers, which signify the fourteen fearlessnesses (*caturdaśa-araṇā*) that delight sentient beings. This is the functioning [of the essence]. From... [the essence].

The manifestation of the essence is like a lotus emerging from a pond; that within the flower there is a woman symbolizes unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*). This universal movement proceeds through compassion, like a flower supporting a woman.
The woman holds musical instruments to represent the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*):

the *vīṇā* (lute) clarifies that the teaching of Buddha-nature is not uniform; the five hundred instruments demonstrate the manifold ways of attracting sentient beings; and the presence of ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks signifies the integration of others through shared activities (*samānārthatā*).

All beings gathered here return to the fundamental principle; the elephant’s trunk bears flowers, signifying that what is illumined is the perfect cause, wherein there is nothing that is not the wondrous condition.
The red pearls represent the ultimate reality that is most venerable. The flowers that have not yet bloomed signify the perfect cause containing the fruit.

One should know that although the wondrous marks are manifold, they are but a single thought-moment of ignorance. Although phenomena arise through the causal conditions of dharma-nature, they appear as external forms.
The realm of others is precisely the seeing of the inner mind’s wondrous emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, wherein there is no distinction between internal and external.
The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings. To answer regarding the ultimate reality while discussing manifold phenomena:

because the substance inherently possesses all dharmas, cultivation is entirely formed from nature; only when each and every thing is non-arising does the pervasiveness of that substance become manifest.
△ Second, the two views below clarify the text on the ability of wondrous practice to manifest [the truth], in four parts: first, the manifestation of the Perfect Teaching;
second, the arising of marks to symbolize the Dharma; third, the Bodhisattvas’ praise and consolation; fourth, the conclusion establishing the realm.
Having seen these matters, one should again repent with a sincere heart, contemplating and reflecting upon the Mahāyāna mind without ceasing or slackening.

That which can manifest is the illumination; as it is taught and as it truly is, this is called the essential substance (*vastu*). If the perfect practice has not yet been manifested, do not cease your repentance.

This is the practice of practice; this is the true contemplation of the correct path. When the correct [path] and the auxiliary [practices] mutually support one another, the wondrous conduct becomes increasingly manifest. Thus it is said.
To have a "sincere mind" means to penetrate to the source of awakening and reach the wondrous ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

To "contemplate with earnestness" means that when the real mind is bound to its object, both subject and object are forgotten; because the object and the contemplation are in accord without any intervening distraction, it is said that there is no cessation or abandonment.

△ Second, regarding the manifestation of the dharmas of the *vijñapti*: the thesis is established, the essence is revealed, and the pure characteristics arise. This section of the text is divided into twelve parts:

first, "seeing the flowers bloom" and so forth, which expresses the practitioner’s cultivation and realization; second, "the elephant trunk and the red lotus" and so forth, which expresses Samantabhadra’s [realization] for both self and others;
third, "the practitioner having seen it" and so forth, which expresses the presentation of the request upon seeing the signs.
Upon seeing the flowers, they immediately blossomed with golden light and golden radiance;

their lotus pedestals were made of *candana* (Jintusha) jewels, while their flower garlands were formed of Brahma-mani gems and their filaments of diamond (*vajra*) jewels. Within them, one saw transformation Buddhas seated upon the lotus pedestals and numerous bodhisattvas seated upon the lotus filaments.
From the space between the eyebrows of these transformation Buddhas, golden light also issued forth and entered the elephant’s trunk.
From within the elephant's trunk he entered and emerged from its eye; from within its eye he entered and emerged from its ear;

from within its ear he emerged and illuminated the top of the elephant’s head, whereupon he manifested a golden platform above the elephant's head. Upon this platform appeared three transformed persons:
one grasping a golden wheel, one holding a maṇi jewel, and one wielding a vajra-pestle. As the one raised the pestle and aimed it at the elephant, the elephant was immediately able to walk.
Without treading upon the ground, he traversed the void, hovering seven feet above it. Upon the ground were the marks of his footprints;
within each footprint, the thousand spokes and rims were all perfectly complete. Between each rim, a great lotus flower sprang forth.

Upon each of these lotus flowers, a transformation elephant appeared, also possessing seven limbs. Following the movements of the great elephant, as its feet were raised and lowered, seven infant elephants were born.
Accompanied by his retinue, he followed the great elephant.

Through cultivation and realization, he further manifested the fourfold [wisdoms]: first, the Flower-Spreading Terrace appeared to symbolize the provisional aspect of phenomena (*saṃvṛti*), while the golden light revealed the ultimate reality of principle (*paramārtha*).

This golden light is the quiescent illumination of *dharmatā*; the flower terrace upon which one may sit is the very principle that is to be realized through profound contemplation—the *cintāmaṇi* (Vaiḍūrya).
"Jewel" (*ratna*) here refers to the red-colored jewel; "Brahma-maṇi" here means "pure and stainless," which is also a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).

Taking this as a garland symbolizes the mutual reflection of wondrous wisdom. The *vajra* serves as the stamen, symbolizing that the fundamental cause—the original principle and its objective realm—is about to unfold.

Regarding the two Buddhas sitting upon lotus flowers and so forth: this signifies that the perfect, eternal initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is in profound accord with the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

The Bodhisattva’s sitting upon the lotus represents that myriad wholesome conditions and causes provide the adornment for the principle of the fruit; the white hair-tuft between the eyebrows signifies the Middle Way, where the golden light manifests as the wisdom of principle.

From entering the elephant’s trunk up to the golden platform, it demonstrates the application of principle and wisdom to universally purify all faculties, revealing that the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the basis of the Dharma-realm, and symbolizing the perfection of wisdom and practice. This constitutes the third transformation.

The person represents the three wisdoms abiding at the peak of the untainted; the vajra represents the wondrous emptiness; the wheel manifests the emergence from the provisional; and the jewel indicates the Middle Way.
Raising the vajra and pointing it toward the image signifies that the practitioner guides their conduct toward the principle. Emptiness-wisdom is the foundation;

"feet not treading the ground" means that the calculations of the four natures have been forgotten. "Treading the void while wandering" refers to the practice of non-action, advancing beyond [dualistic extremes].

The ground seven feet [deep] represents the seven circular factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), which can bring one away from the ground of birth and death. Where there are marks of seals upon the ground, they seal the two grounds of death;
where there are none, it is the true reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, the hundred realms are opened and clarified, and the thousand suchnesses are manifested;

therefore, it is said that the thousand spokes, hubs, and rims are all fully complete. The four transformations follow from practice, and the hundred realms and thousand dharmas are now, through the opening of this sutra, all brought to fulfillment.
The Buddha-way is such that within each and every spoke of the wheel, a lotus flower arises and a transformed elephant appears;

this signifies the fulfillment of the perfect cause through the seven branches. These are the seven purities revealed by the fruit: namely, purity of precepts, mind, view, abandonment of doubt, discernment, practice, and nirvana.
Because these seven purities extend to the lower causes, it is said "there are also [the practices]. Since their conduct is identical to that of Samantabhadra, it is said:

"You are called a 'Dharma-son' because you practice the Mahāyāna. This is a concluding praise of his merit. To follow the teaching and practice the Way is to ensure that the lineage of the Dharma is not severed.
Now, regarding the discussion of "lineage" (*gotra*), there are different categories of nature.

If one speaks of not being separated from the five desires, not severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the twelve matters of suffering, such meanings correspond to the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*). From these three causes, the Tathāgata and [the Bodhisattvas] are born.

Therefore, the text below states: "The Buddha’s three bodies arise from the Vaipulya; they give rise to the three kinds of pure bodies of the Buddha."
Furthermore, "giving birth" refers to the lineage of the Buddha (*buddhagotra*), and "not severing" refers to the lineage of the Dharma (*dharmagotra*). However, the lineage of the Saṃgha is lacking;

One should know that by bringing these to fulfillment, the lineage of the Sangha shall not be severed; for the Vaipulya sutras are the life-force of all Buddhas and the root of Bodhi.

How could one not diligently practice them? Just as a mountain begins with a single basket of earth and a tree of a hundred-cubit girth starts from a single hair, the Bodhi of the three Buddhas has never been attained without passing through this.
Third, it is shown that the object and the contemplation are inseparable, for it is precisely because of the power of contemplation [that the object is realized].

First, there are four initial features: first, the ground; second, the jewel trees; third, the light of the seats; and fourth, the bodhisattvas.
Although one wishes to contemplate the Buddha, one must first rely upon these supports; this is the necessary and correct sequence.

The "thorns" are severed afflictions, views, and craving; "lapis lazuli" is the source of awakening, pure and clear; the "interspersed" refers to the adornment of various virtues.
Although these are said to be signs perceived within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how could they deviate from the dharma-gate of mental contemplation?

Thus, the Sūtra says: "If one levels the mind-ground, then the ground of the world will all become level. As for the "trees," this is the collective name for all woods; "high and wondrous" refers to their excellence.
The tree’s form is precious and beautiful, manifesting the Tathāgata’s perfect conduct that transcends all stages;

its gold and silver signify the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth, while the seven jewels represent the seven factors of enlightenment of non-arising. How could such wondrous practice be shared by others?
The light upon the seat is inconceivable, not arising from mental volition; therefore it is called "spontaneous," and when a fearless person sits upon it, it is named the Lion Throne.
The wondrous realm of the Way transcends both the ultimate and conventional truths; it rises twenty *yojanas* high.

Its fundamental principle is the hundred realms, termed "eternal quiescent illumination" (*nitya-śānta-prakāśa*), which is called the light of a hundred jewels. The five hundred white elephants represent the five Buddha-natures;
that the hundred realms are empty and fused, originally and eternally pure, is signified by them. That each possesses Samantabhadra signifies the arising of function from the single true path.

The former was a general teaching of the Dharma, whereas this is the specific exposition of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The former was the path of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mārga*).
Still dim regarding the benefits of present dhyāna, one subsequently awakens and beholds [the Buddha] because of having attained vision through yearning and longing.
The Buddha is called the "Hero of the World" (Lokavīra) because he is a supreme man (*puruṣottama*) who has long been free from feminine weakness;

Because it illuminates through and through, he addressed Mount Qi and offered words requesting a manifestation; having been requested, he appeared.

When the text speaks of "voice-hearers" (*śrāvaka*), this is discussed provisionally based on those who follow from questioning, yet it must necessarily include Bodhisattvas as well. Once the matters of the *Lotus Sūtra* are concluded, one should return to the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*);
why then does the gaze still behold Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa? The answer is that the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is perfected with the serene light (*śāntaprabhā*) as its essence.

The wondrous essence of reality is profound and serene, extending to the end of the future; yet when the fires of sentient beings' karma have not been extinguished, one perceives the kalpa coming to an end and being consumed by flames.
If the Buddha-wisdom within the mind-ground is level and smooth, then the Buddha-land is eternally pure.
That our Great Master of Tiantai personally practiced this Dharma and was able to see Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the great assembly is precisely in accord with the sutras; this is truly to be believed.

The Bodhisattvas who serve as their retinues each practice the same conduct as Samantabhadra;

This current passage shows the wondrous function, clarifying that the path of Samantabhadra is identical for both [the provisional and the ultimate]. Both are *siddhāntas* (established tenets) based on the causal stage.

Through great awakening, one attains the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various *dhāraṇī* gates.
From the first character, white light radiates from the *ūrṇā-kośa* and enters the practitioner’s mind-moments;

because this light of the Middle Way enters the heart of repentance, it causes one to remember past virtues as clearly as if looking with one's own eyes, like one possessing the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Thus it is said.

It appears that this is a comparison to the true [state] and a realization of even deeper benefit; thus, one awakens to the *dhāraṇī*. Regarding the question: "The hundred-thousandfold *parivarta-dhāraṇī* has already been realized above; why is it stated again here? The answer is:

the preceding text provisionally addressed those of medium capacity who emerge into the provisional (*upāya-niḥsaraṇa*); now, fearing there may be others following from the inferior capacity, it is repeated.
Furthermore, *parivarta-dhāraṇī* is a general term for what is attained through realization, whereas "hundred-thousandfold" specifically points to other gates.
Arising from samādhi, he beheld all the emanated Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath various jewel trees;
he further saw clusters of exquisite lotuses on the lapis lazuli ground, which surged forth from the space below,
with as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a speck of dust sitting cross-legged amidst each flower, and he also saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s emanations present there.
Within the assembly, they praise and expound the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "arising" within the context of the marks of vision, it means that while quiescent, there is constant illumination. As for seeing the emanation bodies, this is because the Dharma of Repentance is about to be proclaimed;
they have gathered together as witnesses. The clusters of wondrous lotuses represent the perfect cause of identical essence, manifesting the supreme practices of the Tathāgata.
The wondrous principle of *Sukhāvatī* (the Land of Peace and Light) signifies that within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) completely becomes cultivation;
thus it is said that they "emerge. Regarding each individual flower: "causes" are identical, while the "Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust" represent the unity of practice.

The emanations of Samantabhadra, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, praise and expound the Mahāyāna, thereby revealing the intent of transformation. Question: How does the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) herein compare to that above?
Question: Regarding the phrase "awakening and seeing," how does it respond to the preceding text? Answer: "Awakening and seeing" refers to remaining within meditative concentration;

now, arising from that concentration and generating faith is the emergence from dhyāna. Question: How do these compare with the "earth-surging" [bodhisattvas] in the *Lotus Sūtra*—are they the same or different?

Answer: That passage clarifies the cause and conditions for manifesting the original state through emanated forms; here, it shows the prior cultivation of practitioners as a prelude to the wondrous repentance.
△ They were instructed to practice the six recollections.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, with one voice and in unison, instructed the practitioners to purify their six sense faculties;
some said, "You should recollect the Buddha," some said, "You should recollect the Dharma," and others said, "You should recollect the Sangha."
Some may say, "You should mindfully recollect the precepts"; some may say, "You should mindfully recollect generosity"; or some may say, "You should mindfully recollect the heavens.
Those who speak with one voice in unison shall together proclaim the path of repentance, while those who speak individually shall provide instruction according to what is appropriate for each.
To recollect the Buddha is to perfectly illumine the three bodies; to recollect the Dharma is to profoundly fathom the true mark;

to recollect the Sangha is for phenomena and principle to be non-dual; to recollect the precepts is for inherent virtue to be without fault; to recollect renunciation is for wealth and the Dharma to be without attachment;

and to recollect the heavens is to wondrously contemplate the ultimate truth. When these six recollections settle the mind, the faculties and their objects are easily purified. [This concludes] the extensive explanation of the six recollections.

As stated in the aforementioned sūtra (and so forth), these six mindfulnesses of the Buddha can immediately lead to the mindfulness of the Dharma; this mindfulness of the Dharma is the mindfulness of the objective realm (*ālambana-dharma*).
The mindfulness of the Saṃgha is the mindfulness of the practice (*pratipatti-dharma*). The [remaining] three [mindfulnesses] may be understood accordingly.
