by clinging to the sensory object of sound, the apertures of the senses remain unclarified, like glue adhering to grass. Not only is the object of sound adhered to, but one should know that the three evil realms are likewise adhered to.
Alas! The pitfall of the sense-faculties and their objects ensnares people in such a manner. Having understood this, next—

Seeking repentance through the realization that the fundamental nature is eternally enlightened is called "awakened awareness. Because one dares not conceal the turbid evils of beginningless time, they must be fully disclosed;
following the preceding analogy, it should be said: "May the water of wisdom grant me cleansing."
△ Fourth, the vision of the signs:
Having finished the repentance, one sees the Buddha Prabhūtaratna emitting a great radiance;

this golden light shines everywhere throughout the eastern direction and the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodies of the immeasurable Buddhas are likewise of true golden color. In the sky of the eastern direction, this proclamation is made:
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, is named Śubhavyūha, and there are also countless emanated Buddhas seated beneath jewel trees on lion thrones in the full lotus posture.
All these World-Honored Ones have entered the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms and all speak these words:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are now reading and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras."
That which you recite is the realm of the Buddha. The text is divided into three parts.
First, regarding the light illuminating the ten directions: there are three kinds of light—first, the light of color;

second, the light of wisdom; and third, the light of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Wherever these lights shine, the ten directions are brilliantly illuminated. Next, regarding the voice from the void in the eastern direction:
This concludes the accomplishment of the preceding merit and gives rise to the subsequent realm. The Way of all Buddhas is the same;

there is a model of a manifested Buddha named Śubhavyūha (Good Virtue), who constantly delights in the ultimate. Third, "All World-Honored Ones enter samādhi" demonstrates the identity of their practice.
The name of this concentration is "Universal Manifestation," meaning it pervades every single atom of all lands. It also offers praise.
Reciting the sutras is the realm of the Buddha; there is no liberation to be seen apart from words and letters.

Second, the assistance for accomplishment has three parts: first, revealing the principle to clarify the error; second, establishing contemplation to advance in practice; third, the fruition accomplished and the teaching initiated.
Now, regarding the first, the revelation of the principle: the faculty of the ear is refined and lucid; its nature is fundamentally awakened and profoundly still, unlike wood or stone.

Regarding the error of taking birth as non-extinction: because they turn their backs on the fundamental teaching and follow the flow of sounds, they are like birds caught in a net, pecking at one thing only to abandon it for another.
Because ordinary beings are driven by the habitual tendencies of karma toward sound, at the time of death they first see waves and floods, drowning heaven and earth;
when the spirit descends, they ride the current into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two further states.

The first characteristic is that when one listens with the gates open, various clamors cause the spirit to become confused and disordered; when one listens with the gates closed, there is silence and nothing is heard, causing the dark soul to sink into oblivion.
When the retribution ends, one is born as a human in a frontier land or falls into wrong views, failing to hear the True Dharma.
Because the habit-energy of extinguished hearing still persists, one may dance to the sound of a lute, with body and mind utterly deluded.
Being disordered, they lack self-composure and fall into the peripheral lands of emptiness, where they do not hear the teachings of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Therefore, even while seated amidst material things, they are like deaf people; though they are Bodhisattvas who receive the provisional teachings, they do not hear them, yet they discriminate among various phenomena and thus fall into the peripheral lands of conventional truth, where they do not hear the Dharma of the Middle Way.
Even regarding the teaching of the Great Perfect Nirvana, they have as yet not heard it.

What else could this be but wrong view? Such people as these are all deluded regarding the nature of hearing, or they are stuck in birth and death, or stuck in the partial truth, or stuck in the merely provisional, or stuck in the merely middle; clinging everywhere, they fall into the two progressive paths of birth and death.
If one wishes to be liberated from them, one must realize that the ear, sound, and consciousness are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*).
There is no creator and no recipient; it is undifferentiated from the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Because external suffering is applied through the union of the primary and auxiliary practices, the karmic burdens of the ear-organ can be dissolved and purified.

Once the three fruits are established—the middle two and the first—then, immediately within the ear-organ, one rides a great vehicle that moves without shifting, and the dust of afflictions is eliminated.

True illumination does not destroy the faculty of hearing, yet it enables one to hear universally; whether entering meditative absorption or emerging from it to speak, seeing forms or perceiving touch, all are attained with mastery.
Subsequently, when initiating the teaching, one employs the faculties and their objects to perform Buddha-work, causing all beings to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
This Dharma-gate of the ear-faculty encompasses everything—vertically deep and horizontally vast.

Inconceivable. △ Third, from "Having spoken these words" onwards, the section on the nose-faculty also has four parts: first, the explanation of the scriptural text; second, the assistance in its accomplishment. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, Samantabhadra’s instruction on repentance; second, the confession of offenses in accordance with those instructions.
Having spoken these words, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva further explained the method of repentance:

"In immeasurable kalpas of your past lives, because of your craving for fragrances, you differentiated various consciousnesses and became attached to them everywhere, falling into the cycle of birth and death.
You should now contemplate the cause of the Mahāyāna; the cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."

The first section has two parts: first, connecting the preceding to the following; second, clarifying the transgression and revealing the core doctrine. This also has two parts: first, a brief clarification of the characteristics of the transgression;

second, a subtle revelation of the Perfect Doctrine (*yuanzong*). Regarding the description of the characteristics: "discriminating the various consciousnesses" means that because of smelling the fragrance, the other five consciousnesses are stirred.
For instance, the fragrance of a male or female body then draws forth the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), while the fragrance of delicacies and meals likewise draws it forth.

The movement of the tongue-consciousness and all such movements follow this same principle. For immeasurable kalpas, beings have been deluded and failed to understand, causing the eight hundred merits to become obscured and vanish.
Consequently, they do not perceive the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s body or the fragrance of his merits;
having lost the Buddha’s nose, they fall into the various realms of existence. To extinguish the offenses of the nose and manifest its merits, one should contemplate the causes of the Mahāyāna.
In this Mahāyāna sutra, there is the practice of peaceful conduct with marks (*sanimitta-śānta-caryā*). By means of a mind without marks (*animitta-citta*), one cultivates practices with marks;

both the primary path and the auxiliary paths all point to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the perfect cause. Within the hundred realms, the three truths are all emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.
Just as in a *campaka* grove one does not smell any other fragrance, so it is with the perfect cause; the perfect fruit is likewise so.
The *Śāstra* says: "If the illumination of an object by a lamp is identical before and after [its lighting]," △ Second, confessing one's transgressions in accordance with the teaching:
Having heard these words, one should prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and further repent. Once the repentance has been performed, one should speak as follows:
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to the Stūpa of Many Treasures! Homage to all the emanated Buddhas of Śākyamuni throughout the ten directions!
Having spoken these words, they universally prostrated to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the Buddha Virtuous Virtue of the East and to all his emanated Buddhas!
Prostrating with every thought as if seeing them directly before one's eyes, they made offerings of incense and flowers, making offerings to each and every one.
Having finished, they knelt with palms joined and praised the Buddhas with various verses.
Having offered praise, they spoke of the ten non-virtuous actions to repent for their transgressions. Having repented, they spoke these words:

"In immeasurable kalpas of past lives, out of craving for tastes, fragrances, and tactile objects, I committed many evils. Because of these causes and conditions, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have constantly suffered."
Today we reveal and confess these unwholesome karmas— those of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, the borderlands,
and those with wrong views— and turn toward the Buddhas, the Kings of the True Dharma, to speak of our transgressions and repent.
The text consists of four parts. First, within the confession of transgressions, "I take refuge in all Buddhas" means to request their empowerment and protection.
As the text states, next, "single-mindedly prostrating" means that both body and mind are fully engaged. Both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration are equally empty and quiescent.
Among all the Buddhas in the lands of the ten directions, there is not one who does not receive this prostration. The Buddhas do not come; they come to my place of practice.
Neither departing nor arriving at the buddha-fields, thus the karma of the body is detached from the nature of bodily karma;
with the prior and subsequent limits severed, one enters the ocean of the Dharma-realm. This is called practicing the offering of Dharma.

Incense leaves behind its odor to become the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*), while flowers delight the nature to become wisdom. With various verses of praise, as if in peaceful meditation, one joins the palms for ten million [eons].
In verse, he praises the King of All Dharmas, the inconceivable King of Vows whose three karmas are perfected. Through the three periods [of the day], he sets forth his various transgressions;

previously, he analyzed the various consciousnesses, whereas now he universally repents for the ten non-virtuous actions. Fourth, having already performed the confession, he further provides a specific summary in two parts.
First, he demonstrates the former delusions; the text cites the three evil realms as a specific discussion of retribution. If, regarding odors or tastes...
Contact gives rise to anger; those who harbor anger receive an unwholesome body in hell. Those who give rise to greed receive the body of a hungry ghost.
Those who give rise to delusion receive the body of an animal. Discussing the retribution in general: through anger one falls into the three evil realms; greed and delusion are likewise.
Although fragrance is a minor matter, people do not realize this; few recognize that attachment to it invites retribution. It is as follows:

The following section concludes the current discourse on the confession of all offenses related to the sense organ of the nose. Among all dharmas, this constitutes the King within the Dharma-treasury.
Because the Buddhas have entered into this, which governs with sovereign mastery, the Buddha is called the "King. To "return" means to turn back;
to "face toward" means not to turn away. This is the essential method for extinguishing transgressions.

Regarding the first of the two parts on "Aiding Achievement," the initial demonstration of principle is as follows: To begin with, the fundamental nature of the nose-faculty is all-pervasive, fully possessing the five noses of a Buddha, and is originally interfused.

However, those who follow along with external objects fail to realize this due to defiled attachment; it is like honey upon a blade—though the one who craves it delights in it, they wound their tongue.
Therefore, the fault of the ordinary person’s nose-faculty invites evil retribution, such that at the moment of death...

At that time, those who previously saw the poisonous vapors filling the near and far distances perceive the spirits of the deceased leaping from the earth into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two distinct signs:
first, those with open hearing are intensely tormented in mind by being熏 (xūn) by the various evil vapors;

second, those with blocked hearing are stifled by the vapors so they cannot pass through, fainting upon the ground. Those of the Two Vehicles are greedily attached to precepts and meditative concentration.
The fragrances of the five bodies descend into the three unconditioned states, yet those who have not attained the fragrance of the merits of the Buddhas’ liberation cannot perceive them.
Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings distinguish the fragrant merits of various dharmas, perceiving them as the obscured conventional truth;

whereas the fragrance of the Perfect and Sudden teaching, like burning a single pellet that fully possesses all scents, is such that those who have never before smelled it—such people as these [are unable to perceive it].
If one violates this by smelling, the essential knowledge and vision are lost; with inverted perceptions, one revolves in saṃsāra and fails to attain liberation.

If you wish to be freed from these manifold afflictions, you should realize the nature of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) as being free from the conditions of penetration and obstruction. It is quiescent, and its nature—whether fragrance or stench—abides neither within, nor without, nor in between.
It is naturally without breaking or destruction, without abiding and without attachment, identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and free from the nature of discrimination.
Based on this, through repentance, prostration, praise, and offering, the darkness in the nose-faculty [is dispelled] by a single lamp in a dark room. This is able to destroy the three fruits;

the middle two fruits are accomplished, and the first fruit is attained immediately within the nose-faculty. By operating a single precious chariot upon the Great Straight Path, one attains the eight hundred merits immediately before one's eyes.
As for the teacher who initiates the teaching, once the fruits are accomplished, one performs offerings by bestowing fragrant food.
The Buddha’s work universally causes all beings to realize the Samādhi of the Merit-Treasury of Fragrance-Purity.
△ After the confession, the fourth section on the faculty of the tongue has two parts: first, the explanation of the scriptural text;

second, the assistance in its fulfillment. The first part has two sections: first, causing the confession of the faculty of the tongue; second, from "Having done this... onwards, observing the signs in accordance with the confession.
Having already performed repentance, yet with body and mind still not at ease, you should further read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras.
By the power of the Mahāyāna, a voice will sound from the sky, saying: "O Son of the Dharma, you should now praise and expound the Mahāyāna before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
in the presence of all Buddhas, you should confess your own transgressions. The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are your compassionate fathers; you must speak of them yourself."
The unwholesome and evil karma produced by the faculty of the tongue— this faculty of the tongue manifests the signs of evil karma through false speech,
frivolous talk, harsh words, double-tongued speech, slandering, lying, praising wrong views, and speaking useless words; such various and manifold evil karmas,
including inciting strife, destroying harmony, and preaching what is not the Dharma as if it were the Dharma— all these many transgressions, I now fully repent.
Having spoken these words before the World-Heroes, one should prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Joining the palms and kneeling for a long time, one should speak as follows: "The faults of this tongue are immeasurable and boundless; the thorns of all evil karma emerge from the root of the tongue.
It is from this tongue that the True Wheel of Dharma is obstructed, and by such an evil tongue, the seeds of merit are severed in favor of what is not righteous."

He frequently uses various pretexts to forcefully advocate for and praise wrong views; like adding fuel to a fire, he is like a fierce blaze that harms sentient beings, or like one who drinks poison and dies without even a wound.
Such retribution for these evil, perverse, and unwholesome sins shall cause one to fall into the evil realms for hundreds and thousands of kalpas.
Because of such false speech, one falls into the great hells. I now take refuge in and pay homage to all [the Buddhas].
The Buddha reveals his dark evils. First, there are three initial points:
(1) the sound of emptiness instructs through repentance; (2) the instruction recounts verbal transgressions; (3) the third is the binding of the faculty of the tongue. Regarding the first passage:
when body and mind are not indolent, then phenomena and principle operate in tandem. This is because for kalpas past, [he] has engaged in slander.
The True Teaching now extols the Mahāyāna to specifically remedy the transgression of the tongue. Since the Buddha is the compassionate father, sentient beings possess the three causal seeds;
because these exist and can be brought forth, they may be regarded as sons. The Buddha’s three [bodies] exist in the fruit and are termed the "three virtues.
Although cause and effect differ in name, their essential nature is the same. The son urgently addresses the father: "The roots of my transgressions can be uprooted. Thus he recounts his past faults.

In the middle [section], first the four faults of speech are described; next, regarding "false speech" (*mṛṣāvāda*), it is said that "speaking directly" is called *yan* (speech), while "responding in dialogue" is called *yu* (language);
thus, these two are distinguished. To praise wrong views means to cause others to lose right mindfulness by denying cause and effect, as well as falling into the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
To "instigate strife" means to slander one's ruler or father and to create dissension among kinsmen. To "entrap" means...
When a gentleman advances a petty person like Xiao Yu or Wei Yuansong, who sought to destroy Buddhism, such individuals are truly the "heroes" of strife and contention.

If one possesses a fine eloquence yet slaughters sentient beings, drinks wine, eats pungent foods, breaks the fast, or violates the precepts—even if such words do not appear in their texts, they should likewise be repented of;
now we simply speak of "all transgressions," for this is the Buddha’s teaching.
To preach what is the Dharma as non-Dharma, and what is not the Buddha’s Dharma as the Dharma—such a web of inverted delusions is difficult to describe in full.
The Hero of the World [restrained his tongue] once more; for an evil tongue harms others with pain that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones, and thus it is likened to a thorn.
To slander the Dharma and to cause a schism in the Sangha is called "severing the Wheel of Dharma. However, the severing of the True Wheel of Dharma occurs only in...

When a Buddha, such as Tathāgatavighna, preaches the Dharma or requests entry into *parinirvāṇa*, and after the Buddha’s passing, someone obstructs the preaching of the Dharma or seizes the conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha—these are all termed "similar breaking of the Wheel of Dharma" (*cakrabheda-pratirūpaka*).

The details of the five similar *ānantarya* offenses are as described in the *Abhidharmakośa* (and so forth). That which does not accord with correct principle is called "unrighteousness" (*anartha*); it is an attack upon what is heterodox.
To arbitrarily fabricate explanations based on delusion is as described in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*:

"If a preacher gives divergent interpretations—such as explaining that one *droṇa* of water dissolves one *prastha* of curd so that it appears to have the color of curd but has no flavor when eaten—it is because the devas are incensed, and thus the three calamities arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, the Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma without considering the proper time, it is instead called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). All such instances are termed [frivolous speech].
This is not the true meaning; such heterodox teachings are like fire that burns away the seeds of goodness.
To praise them is like adding fuel to the flame, causing false views to flourish ever more intensely. The fires of karma spread and蔓延 (extend), harming sentient beings.

Those who do not follow the Buddha’s teachings of morality, concentration, and wisdom, yet claim to possess a "separate transmission outside the teachings," are for the most part merely heterodox. These evil causes are formless, like drinking poison that remains within.
Dying without having suffered sores, one’s mouth invites evil retributions for hundreds or thousands of kalpas, falling into the great hells to drink molten copper and consume scorched iron balls;
the myriad forms of suffering from being plowed by iron plows upon the tongue cannot be suppressed or endured.
All of these are the self-reproach resulting from the false imaginings of the faculty of the tongue.
△ Second, the manifestation of signs upon making this reflection. Part one: observing the signs and receiving the instruction. This section has four parts;
first, the announcement by a voice from space. While he was reflecting thus, a voice arose in the sky: "In the south there is a Buddha named Candanagandha; that Buddha also..."
Innumerable emanations of all Buddhas all preach the Mahāyāna to eliminate sinful evil.
The Buddha named Candanagandha has perfected the fruits of the four virtues; like fragrance that universally perfumes, he causes all sentient beings to leave behind the stench of the three delusions.
As for his emanations, they are as described in the text.
△ Next, having finished the confession, prostrate once more.
Thus, regarding these various transgressions, one now confesses them with a sincere heart before the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of Great Compassion, throughout the ten directions.
Having spoken these words, one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and bows again to all the Buddhas.

To approach the physical body of birth and death with the ground of the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and thereby accomplish the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*)—this is the meaning of ritual prostration.
One should understand that both form and mind are ungraspable, and thus perform universal prostrations to all Tathāgatas throughout the ocean of lands;

their responsive manifestations are inconceivable, like the mutual reflection of jewels on a celestial crown. Otherwise, I fear it would be like throwing an empty bottle to extinguish a fire, for there is no water within the bottle.
The fire will certainly be difficult to extinguish.
△ Third, the addition of light:
At that time, all Buddhas again emit radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body, causing their body and mind to naturally experience joy.
One gives rise to great compassion, universally mindful of all beings.

When the compassionate light of the Sage shines down upon the practitioner, they give rise to the mind according to their true nature; because they are free from conceptual attachment, it is called "spontaneous" (svayambhū) compassion.
Both of these dharmas are without conditions; they extract the suffering of the essential nature, yet there is no suffering to be extracted.

The bliss of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is such that no other bliss can compare to it; because it bestows [this bliss] and uproots [suffering] throughout the ten dharma-realms, it is called "all-encompassing" (*sarva*).
△ Fourth, the teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the Buddhas extensively taught the practitioner the dharmas of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and also instructed them in kind speech and the cultivation of the six points of mutual respect.

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are called the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*); these four are collectively termed "immeasurable" because they are derived from their objects.
The name [of these immeasurables] is given because the sentient beings who are their objects are infinite; thus, the names that take them as objects are likewise infinite according to those realms.

As for compassion (*karuṇā*), it is as previously described. As for joy (*muditā*), it is the state of mind that rejoices upon seeing others obtain happiness, giving rise to delight, being free from anger, resentment, enmity, and affliction;
such a joyful mind pervades the ten directions. As for equanimity (*upekṣā*), it takes other sentient beings as its object and is without...
To be free from hatred and attachment, as if realizing the tranquility and purity of *nirvāṇa*, is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

These four mental states are fundamentally meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). To bestow upon other sentient beings the extraction of suffering and the granting of happiness—so that these beings truly become free from suffering and truly attain happiness—is taught in detail in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great [Perfection of Wisdom]), and so forth. Teaching through affectionate speech refers to the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*).

Among them, one Bodhisattva uses words that are skillful and gentle to accord with sentient beings, comforting and instructing them so that those who hear may give rise to affection and love, thereby becoming capable of receiving the Way.
Regarding the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*): if a Bodhisattva skillfully employs these six harmonies, they will be in secret accord with all beings;
by making a good beginning and seeing it through to the end, they are able to establish sentient beings in stability.
Regarding those who practice harmony and respect on the path to enlightenment: externally they accord with the virtues of others, while internally they remain humble and self-effacing;

thus it is so named. These are: first, harmony and respect in shared precepts; second, harmony and respect in shared views; third, harmony and respect in shared conduct; fourth, harmony and respect through physical kindness;
fifth, harmony and respect through verbal kindness; sixth, harmony and respect through mental kindness.
△ Second, rejoicing upon receiving the instruction.
At that time, the practitioner hears this exhortation and their heart is filled with great joy; they further recite and practice it without ever flagging or ceasing.

Because they have received the instruction without transgression, their diligent recitation and practice without flagging or ceasing is like one whose head is on fire and who strives to extinguish it.
Second, regarding the three parts for assisting in the accomplishment [of the goal], first is the demonstration of the principle: "The nature of the tongue is awakened as eternal;

fundamentally it is without arising or ceasing, empty throughout the three periods of time, and equal to the Buddha. As for the transgression: it arises from turning one's back on the true awakening—the wondrous, profound, and luminous nature—and by alternating between sweet and bitter [flavors], one falsely gives rise to various evils.
Thus, the flavor of the Buddhas' Dharma, which completely fills the Dharma-realm, cannot be discerned.
Because of attachment to the existence of birth and death, one loses the ultimate truth; because the tongue does not understand that phenomena are eternal, one loses the conventional truth;
because the tongue does not know the Middle Way, one loses the Buddha-tongue. Because of losing the tongue of merit, one merely craves worldly flavors and extensively commits various evils.
The evil karma of the tongue-root invites bitter retribution, such that at the time of death, one first sees iron [hooks].
A net of fierce and blazing flames completely covers the world; the consciousness of the deceased descends through it, suspended head-downward within the Avīci Hell.
Two manifestations arise: first, the inhaled breath forms freezing ice that splits the flesh of the body;
second, the inhaled breath flies forth as fierce fire that scorches and rots the marrow of the bones. Once this retribution is exhausted, one becomes a human again.
Those who are stammering, mute, or speech-impaired lack credibility; they cannot proclaim the profound flavor of the Dharma’s principles, being like dumb sheep.
Those of the Two Vehicles who savor emptiness are like fish frozen in ice; having abandoned the flavor of ambrosia, they cling to the salty, bitter, and sour flavors of impermanence and the like.
Claiming to have attained extinction when they have not, they commit verbal transgressions and drink the poison of ignorance.
Those bodhisattvas of provisional teaching who, out of attachment to change and death, are able to universally distinguish the various medicinal flavors of the mundane and supramundane worlds,
causing people to taste them; and who furthermore repeatedly and in countless ways forcefully preach,
praise, and cling to the biased, false, and provisional as being the "Middle Way" apart from extremes— these are what Vimalakīrti rebukes as holding wrong views.
This is it: only the Buddha alone is the speaker of truth and the speaker of reality; all others speak falsely. Second, as for the contemplation of liberation:
one should realize that the tongue-root is fundamentally true, wondrous, and eternal. Neither objects enter nor does the faculty emerge;
the sense-object and the faculty are perfectly luminous and inconceivable. One should contemplate flavors through the three wondrous contemplations.

Contemplating the inconceivable realm through the eight horizontal and vertical phrases breaks all attachments to inherent natures; by classifying this as the contemplation of the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment, one does not enter [delusion].
Diligently practicing the five repentances causes the defilements and impurities of the tongue-root to be eliminated without remainder.
Thereupon, one mounts the white ox-cart upon the tongue-root and proceeds directly to the treasure-store; thereafter, whatever one consumes shall all be...
Having accomplished the three fruits of ambrosia, he is able to pervade the trichiliocosm with a single wondrous voice;
even until his attainment of Buddhahood and Bodhi, he performs the Buddha-work by tasting with his flavor-sense and manifesting the broad and long tongue to guide and instruct sentient beings.
Next, he establishes the teachings so that all sentient beings, whenever they eat or drink, may know the accumulation of food, know the suffering of food, and know [the nature of] food.
One knows the cessation of nutriment and the cessation of ignorance regarding nutriment, up to and including the cessation of old age and death regarding nutriment;
one also knows the six obscurations regarding nutriment and the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the six perfections regarding nutriment.
One should know that the faculty of the tongue and its objects are a treasury of the Dharma-jewels; this is the true repentance of the tongue-faculty.

In truth, as a sublime guide for both ordinary beings and sages, encompassing phenomena and principle, the provisional and the real, essence and function, self-cultivation and the transformation of others,
and extending vertically through the depths and horizontally across the vastness— it is none other than our own school who can truly recognize this.
△ Furthermore, within the void, there is the fifth [section], the Repentance of Body and Mind, which should likewise consist of four parts.

Examples such as "revealing faults" and "clarifying principles" can be understood from the preceding [sections] and need not be repeated here; I shall now merely explain the text. The text is divided into two parts:

first, the repentance through the empty sound-teachings; second, the locus of the practitioner’s inquiry. The first part is further divided into two: first, showing the characteristics; second, concluding the characteristics.
Furthermore, from within the air, a subtle and wondrous voice spoke these words: "You should now repent with both body and mind.
As for the body, it commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; as for the mind, it dwells upon all unwholesome things, creating the ten evil karmas and the five deeds of immediate retribution.

second, the entry into the stage upon completion of the merit.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extend their right hand to stroke the practitioner’s head and speak these words: “Excellent, excellent!”
"Good son, because you now read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, the Buddhas of the ten directions have taught this method of repentance.

The conduct of a bodhisattva consists in not severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and yet not dwelling in the ocean of the fetters. One contemplates the mind as being without mind, arising from inverted thoughts;
such a thought-mind arises from delusive thoughts, like wind in the sky having no place of dependence. Such is the nature of dharmas."
Neither arising nor perishing, what is sin and what is merit? My own mind is empty; sin and merit have no master.

All dharmas are likewise thus: they neither abide nor perish. To repent in this way—contemplating that the mind is mindless and that dharmas do not abide within dharmas, such that all dharmas are liberated, extinguished, and tranquil—is called the Great Repentance.

Repentance is called adornment; repentance is called the mark of being without transgression; repentance is called the destruction of consciousness. Regarding the first [of these], there are again two parts:
first, the distinct cultivation of the method of contemplation; second, the distinct conclusion of the method of contemplation. Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts:

first, contemplating the king; second, contemplating the subject. Regarding the first of these, there are again three parts. First, as for "non-interruption," it means that awakening and afflictions are non-dual and without distinction.
Specifically, if one were to sever afflictions, that would be the severing of bodhi, because their essence is identical; therefore, it is said that they are not severed.
Furthermore, afflictions are not bodhi, just as a swan king extracts milk from water, because their essences are distinct; therefore, it is said that they do not abide.
Next, to specifically clarify the three contemplations: the true nature of all phenomena is ultimate emptiness, transcending the four and severing the hundred.

Therefore, it is said that "no-mind" is the contemplation of principle (*li*). That which "arises from inversion" refers to the contemplation of phenomena (*shi*), because although the *dharmatā* is fundamentally empty, it exists due to ignorance.
"Thus" means that both phenomenon and principle are centered in the Middle Way: because it is not a phenomenon, it does not arise; because it is principle, it does not perish.
This is the contemplation that is neither phenomenon nor principle. Why? [The text] below examines the mind to detach from attachment.
Regarding sin and merit: the six realms of ordinary beings involve sin, while the four noble stages involve merit. Within the nine realms there is sin, and within the Buddha-realm there is merit;
yet even the sin and merit of the Buddha-realm do not exceed a single thought-moment. The essence of this thought is fundamentally empty. That there is sin and merit is like flowers in the sky:

these flowers have no substantial reality, appearing only because of an eye disease that causes one to perceive flowers where there is only emptiness. If the eye disease is removed, the flowers in the sky immediately vanish. Thus, the mind is the master.

If one realizes that offenses and flowers in the sky are both empty and all things are utterly pure, it is said that one "profoundly penetrates the nature of offenses and blessings, universally illuminating the ten directions.
Furthermore, Lion Bodhisattva said: "Offenses and blessings constitute duality; if one penetrates the nature of offenses, it is no different from the nature of blessings.
To decisively comprehend this characteristic with vajra-wisdom—neither bound nor liberated—is what is meant by 'entering.'"

When examining the gate of non-duality in this manner, outsiders—whether adhering to the single, the manifold, the complete, or the view of wordlessness—as well as those who practice meditation through dark realization, fail to attain the skillful means of the four teachings and four gates;

they mostly fall into deluded emptiness, repudiating cause and effect, and giving rise to views based on emptiness. Their cycle of birth and death becomes vast and boundless; the Tathāgata calls such people "pitiable. All [of these]...

The "Dharma" refers here to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Previously, by examining the sovereign mind through the lens of its emptiness of intrinsic nature, we found it to be without a master;

now, by analogy with the mental factors, the same applies to the sovereign mind. When the root dies, the branches wither; such is the essence of dharmas. Since the mental factors are afflictions, they have no abiding;
since awakening (*bodhi*) has no destruction, this likewise accords with the meaning of being neither interrupted nor abiding. Contemplating that the mind is non-existent...

"Mind" refers to observing the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), wherein the king vanishes; the subsequent passage states that "dharmas do not abide within dharmas," which refers to observing the mental factors (*caitta*), wherein the factors perish.
The mind-king and mental factors are the fundamental cause and root of birth and death.

Since objects arise from conditions, when one now seeks them internally and externally, the object cannot be found; therefore, both the king and the factors vanish. What is called "dharma" here is *dhyāna*.

The *pāramitās* are mental factors (*caitta*), while the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the mind (*citta*). Feeling, perception, and formations are mental factors; the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the mind.
That which is the object of cognition is mental factors; that which is the cognizing subject is the mind. That which is capable of producing is mental factors; that which is produced is the mind.
That which is the境 (*viṣaya*) observed is mental factors; that which is the wisdom (*jñāna*) observing is the mind. Since the mind does not abide by itself, one should know that it is the mind.
"Numbers, as well as sensation, perception, and formations, likewise do not abide"—these "dharmas" refer to the various types of phenomena mentioned above.
Because their nature is empty, there is nothing that can abide; being fundamentally free from conceptualization, they are thus quiescent, and even that which is perceived is extinguished.
Such a conception summarizes [the teaching] by means of the Three Truths: "Great" refers to the Middle Way, and "adornment" refers to the Provisional.
The absence of the marks of transgression is itself emptiness; that which destroys the mind and consciousness is the simultaneous destruction of attachment to these three.

△ Second, the practice: from here below is the section on the completion of effort and entry into the stage. This text has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the supportive accomplishment.
The first part also has two sections: first, the general indication.
Those who perform this repentance attain purity of body and mind and do not abide within any phenomena;
like flowing water, in every moment they behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding the phrase "body and mind": the body encompasses the five sense faculties; because these five faculties are refined and lucid, they are called "pure.
As for "not dwelling in dharmas," this means not dwelling in objective dharmas and not dwelling in cognitive dharmas. It is not that one does not dwell in objective and cognitive dharmas;
rather, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, there is in reality nothing in which to dwell. Because one dwells within Prajñā, one attains [awakening] moment by moment.

Entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) with great swiftness, like a rushing torrent, their minds consist purely of the Dharma and they commune with the spiritual affinity of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
therefore, it is said that they "see. △ Next, the specific demonstration of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored Ones, through the light of great compassion, expounded the dharma of signlessness for the practitioner;
having heard this exposition of the ultimate emptiness, the practitioner’s mind was not startled or terrified, and he immediately entered the stage of the bodhisattva's right determination.

Now, for one who enters emptiness, the preceding mind is the most difficult part; by internally merging with true emptiness and externally relying on the power of the Buddha, one can then enter the stage.
That which is called the "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha) is the reason why it is the true mark (dharmatā). Among all meanings, the true mark is the foremost, and thus it is named the "Ultimate Truth.
A sutra says: "There is karma and there is retribution, yet no agent is perceived; this is called 'emptiness of the ultimate truth' (paramārtha-śūnyatā)."

Because the mind is free from alarm and fear, having penetrated to the depths of the three truths, one is not startled upon hearing them; because it extends to the limits of the Dharma-realm, one is not terrified upon listening to them.
Furthermore, because one has already attained attachment through hearing and reflection, one is not startled; because the merit of the wisdom of cultivation is perfected, one is not terrified.
When subject and object are suddenly extinguished and the cultivated and the innate merge, one wondrously realizes non-arising and ascends to the stage of *sāgaramegha*.

Regarding those who enter the stage through supportive accomplishment, the Sūtra states: "Contemplating the dharma of signlessness and thus corresponding accordingly, one gives rise to no dualistic understanding;
at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately achieves perfect awakening. The Commentary states:

"Before abiding [in the stages], an ordinary person must cultivate four dharmas before being able to enter this stage—namely, generating the mind, practicing cultivation, great compassion, and skillful means. In the present Sūtra, these are represented by burning incense and scattering flowers.

To give rise to the Mahāyāna intention is precisely the arousal of the bodhicitta; to read, recite, repent, and attain right concentration is the meaning of "upholding," which corresponds to the practice of cultivation.
To spontaneously rejoice and give rise to great compassion is Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

For the Buddhas to place their hands upon one’s head and preach the Perfect Emptiness (*paripūrṇa-śūnyatā*) is the True Expedient Means (*upāya*). Because this sutra possesses these four dharmas, one enters the stage of the Right Position (*samyaktva-niyāma*). — *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).

Regarding the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra-vyākhyāna*, it is said that the five grades (*pañca-piṭaka*) within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are somewhat difficult to discern in their underlying intent;

consequently, each grade was divided into two to correspond with the ten stages of faith. Furthermore, the *Mohe zhiguan* states that the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra-vyākhyāna* treats the five grades as the ten stages of faith.
Although the Great Master [Zhiyi] remarked that they were "difficult to discern," the Record Master [Zhanran] did not elaborate on this point nor provide a specific marking (*diǎn*) for it.

Since this present commentary deals with the ten kinds of signs of realization that precede the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), I have not dared to arbitrarily identify the passage concerning the five stages (*pañca-vastu*) in relation to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); I leave this for future scholars.
△ The Buddha spoke below, concluding by revealing the wondrous efficacy through the path of repentance.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "A practitioner who acts in this manner is called one who practices repentance.
This repentance is the method of repentance practiced by all Buddhas of the ten directions and all great Bodhisattvas."
As stated in the text.
△ Furthermore, from "The Buddha again told... onwards, as the sutra draws to a close, the Tathāgata again exhorts and praises; as detailed above, this has already occurred many times.
Even in Confucian texts it is said that one should go to a matter a second and even a third time, let alone in the subtle Way of the Buddha.
That [the Buddha] further exhorts and praises it is because he wishes to cause practitioners to give rise to a heart of profound reverence.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples wish to repent of their evil and unwholesome karma, they should simply read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras;
these Vaipulya sūtras are the eyes of all Buddhas, and all Buddhas rely upon them."
One attains the five eyes and the three bodies of a Buddha; born from the Vaipulya sūtras, this is the Great Dharma Seal.
Within this ocean of Parinirvāṇa, the three kinds of pure Buddha-bodies can arise.

These three bodies are the field of merit for devas and humans, the most supreme among those worthy of offerings. Know that whoever reads and recites the Mahāvaipulya scriptures possesses the merits of a Buddha.
All evils are eternally extinguished as they arise from the Buddha’s wisdom.
This passage consists of three parts: first, citing the practice to encourage cultivation; second, praising the merit of the sutra; and third, concluding with praise for those who uphold it.

Regarding the first part, it says, "One should simply recite it. While the preceding text presented the exposition, this section provides the essential requirements for the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful and Joyful Practice).

One must certainly be free from delusion. Regarding the method of reciting the sutras, it is as the Great Master [Zhiyi] taught in "Contemplating the Mind while Reciting the Sutra" (as detailed therein).

Next, as for the eulogy: the One Vehicle is the ultimate essential and the root of all practices; it is by means of this that all Buddhas have attained perfect enlightenment, and its merit is profoundly deep.
It is for these reasons that one offers praise. This is the Eye of all Buddhas; do not depart from the written words when speaking of the Buddha.

The eye is also the nature of letters being detached; this is precisely the Buddha-eye. Regarding the five eyes: the mundane eye and the lettered eye are phenomena produced by causes and conditions, which constitute the fleshly eye and the celestial eye.
The eye of emptiness is the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*). The eye of phenomena is the provisional [truth], and the Buddha-eye is the Middle Way.
A detailed analysis of the five eyes is as found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-ṭīkā* (and so forth). How could it be that only the five eyes derive from the Vaipulya [sūtras]?
The three—birth, dharma, and retribution—are also born from this; is it not said that they are "born from the mouth of the Buddha"?
Regarding the seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), there are four seals. What is here called "Great" is intended to distinguish them from the three seals of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

If one follows the revelation and clarification, these constitute the single seal of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), wherein nothing is not the true aspect. This is extensively explained in texts such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, etc. (and so forth).
The One Vehicle’s three virtues are termed *parinirvāṇa*; because they are both profound and vast, it is called the "ocean. Regarding this "within such an ocean":
this refers to the principle-nature (*li-xing*) as that which gives rise [to the three virtues], for all three are fully cultivated through practice; thus it is said to "give rise to the three kinds.
Furthermore, when the teaching speaks of the true reality (*shixiang*), the teaching itself is called a "seal" (*yin*); because the seal contains all phenomena, the teaching is also called a "seal."

This is because the present text praises the teaching; these three kinds of bodies are the basis upon which all ordinary beings and sages rely to plant the seeds of merit, and since there is nothing superior to them, they are called "supreme.

Even hearing other sutras yields merit equal to that of making offerings to all Buddhas—surpassing the merit of three Ganges-sands of Buddhas—let alone this sutra, which speaks of ten chapters after three periods of silence.

To praise [this] means that all evils within the fetters are eternally extinguished, which is the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*); that it is born from the Buddha’s wisdom is the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*);
and having attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma, one becomes a true son of the Buddha.
△ At that time, the second verse-text below is divided into two parts: first, twelve and a half lines each eulogize the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) to demonstrate their locations;
next, two lines generally eulogize the six sense organs to show how delusion arises; finally, half a line concludes with an exhortation.
Within the first section, there are six sub-sections repeated as verses; in each individual verse, there is a demonstration of the location. First, one and a half lines eulogize [the first organ].
Regarding the eye faculty:
at that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one's eye faculty is obscured by the hindrance of evil karma and is impure, one should simply recite the Mahāyāna and contemplate the ultimate truth."
This is called the confession that exhausts all unwholesome karma.
The first two phrases cite the faults and obstacles common to the three faculties; "evil" refers to retributive karma as well as afflictions. The next two phrases indicate the locus:

recitation belongs to the realm of signs (*sanimitta*), while mindfulness belongs to the signless (*animitta*). The unification of signs and the signless is the essential method for extinguishing offenses.
The following two lines provide the conclusion.
△ Second, two lines of verse on the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*):
The ear-faculty hears chaotic sounds that destroy the meaning of harmony; from this, madness arises, like that of a deluded monkey.
One should simply recite the Mahāyāna contemplation on the emptiness and signlessness that forever exhausts all evils, so that the divine ear hears throughout the ten directions.
The first line cites instances where hearing disruptive sounds causes confusion; these five types of sounds delude the auditory consciousness.
From the seer Śikhin listening to singing at the beginning, to Kāśyapa hearing the lute and rising to dance at the end—though their levels of depth differ, they were all disturbed by sound.
The meaning of "harmony" (*saṃgraha*) also encompasses the profound: if things are harmonious, the multitude becomes one like water and milk;
yet if one hears of divisive speech (*paiśunya*), conflict immediately arises. If there is harmony in principle, the three truths are identical in essence.

If one hears only of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or the partial provisional (*prajñapti*), erroneous views will arise. The first two phrases below indicate that the locus [of delusion] is eternally exhausted; the latter two phrases provide the conclusion.

As for the further development of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), it should logically comprise five aspects; moreover, this is discussed specifically with respect to the "heavenly" [divine] ear, which is indeed the Buddha’s divine ear.
[Verse 3.2]: Regarding the nose:

the olfactory faculty clings to various fragrances, and following these defilements, various tactile sensations arise. Thus, through such delusion, the nose follows after defilements to produce various sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
If one recites Mahāyāna sūtras and contemplates phenomena as they truly are, one will forever leave behind all evil karma and will not be reborn in future lives.
The first line cites the fault: because of smelling fragrances, the other sense faculties are stirred; thus it says "all tactile sensations.
The preceding text states that "those who were lying down all rise," which refers to the arising of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*). The following two lines indicate the location [of the practice].
To contemplate the sense organs and their objects as being identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—each and every one entering the juncture of suchness—is the Middle Way.
It is the eternal departure from the lower fetters; it benefits the Buddha’s nose and manifests that, being free from the牵引 (inducing force) of karma, there is no further rebirth.
△ Fourth, one and a half verses on the tongue faculty:
If the tongue faculty gives rise to the five kinds of unwholesome karma of harsh speech, and if one wishes to discipline and harmonize oneself,
one should diligently cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and contemplate the true meaning of quiescence, free from all marks of conceptual discrimination.

The first two lines enumerate five types of faults: in addition to the four verbal transgressions, one adds the slander of the True Dharma; the fault of the tongue is immeasurable, and these five all encompass [the transgressions].

If one wishes to descend to the next line to indicate the locus, "self-discipline and compliance" means being compliant with one's original nature, turning away from defilement and uniting with awakening.
The Buddha has no other mind than a mind of compassion; compassion is bodhi.
This is the root of the mind; therefore, it further exhorts one to practice. However, the text briefly summarizes the benefits.
△ Fifth, one and a half lines concern the faculty of mind (*manas*).
"The thoughts of the mind are like a monkey; there is not a single moment they pause. If you wish to subdue them, you should diligently recite the Mahāyāna."
The recitation of the Buddha is accomplished through the power and fearlessness of the Great Awakened Body (*mahābuddhakāya*).
The first half-verse identifies the transgression, while the subsequent verse indicates the locus. Regarding the "Great Awakened Body," one should be endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The *Chanmen* (Gate of Meditation) states: "Those who harbor evil thoughts and deliberations should recollect the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*); the Buddha arises from immeasurable merit. Now...
This concludes the citation of the Ten Powers and the Four Fearlessnesses.
△ Sixth, the three-line verse on the faculty of the body:
The body is the master of the mechanism, like dust swirling with the wind; amidst the play of the six thieves, it moves with sovereign ease and without obstruction.

If you wish to extinguish these evils and forever leave behind all worldly afflictions, dwelling eternally within the city of Nirvana with a mind of tranquil bliss, you should recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and keep in mind the mothers of the Bodhisattvas and their immeasurable, supreme skillful means;
these are attained through contemplation of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The first line raises the issue of the primary agent of the mechanism. In Master Guangming’s commentary, it is pointed out that karma is the primary root, while consciousness is like the observer.
In the present text, it appears as if the body itself is taken as the primary agent; yet the sense objects revolve according to the wind, like a wooden puppet pulled by strings.

If the fruit is dragged along by the cause of karma, the six thieves act wantonly within the faculties to create karmic delusions; there is no dharma that can restrain them. This is called [the state of being] "without restraint."
The next line, "Without hindrance," indicates the cultivation of causes; "the various afflictions" refers to the eighty-four thousand diverse [defilements].

As for the "city of nirvāṇa," it is because one contemplates the true mark of the body and the profound, firm principle of quiescence can prevent what is non-virtuous that it is metaphorically described as a city.
The next line concludes with an exhortation: the first two phrases exhort all bodhisattvas.
Since all [teachings] arise from the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, the Sūtra says: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas;

skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) is the father. This is cited here as an exhortation. The next two lines conclude the discussion on skillful means: these are the excellent expedients by which the Sage transforms sentient beings;
yet they possess the functional application of the Dharma that can penetrate the distinctions between the secret and the wondrous—these three aspects of skillful means constitute the gateway.

Because the five periods encompass the eight teachings, they are called "immeasurable. In reality, the single dharma of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is fully endowed with all dharmas. It may be that one does not attain them;
however, if one should attain them, then within the one, one understands the immeasurable, and within the real, one understands the provisional.

Therefore, this is cited to conclude the repentance for the offenses of the six sense organs. Regarding the passage on designating their locations: the eye is called the "primary truth" (*paramārtha*), and the ear is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

The nose without marks is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi); the body is called the "meaning of true stillness"; the intention is called the "body of great awakening"; and the body is called the "city of nirvāṇa.
Although these six names differ, they are all but the true mark (dharmatā). Let the student not be deluded regarding the essence by means of these names.
△ Next, a summary verse on the arising of delusion:
These six dharmas are called the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). All oceans of karmic obstacles arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can eliminate.
Therefore, one should with a sincere mind repent of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
The first line points to the source from which delusion arises; the six sense organs are that which can produce delusion, while the ocean of karmic obstructions is that which is produced by delusion.
Within the six classes of ordinary beings and the nine realms, there is a river of cyclic rebirth that repeatedly submerges sentient beings, leaving them vast and helpless.
The limits [of existence] are like flowers in the sky, arising from the void; because this perception is not true, there is the cycle of transmigration.

The first line demonstrates the method for extinguishing delusion. Of the two initial phrases, "sitting upright" generally indicates the physical posture, while "contemplating the true mark" directly indicates the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).
By means of the three inconceivable contemplations, one illuminates the subtle and wondrous.

The three truths encompass both phenomena and principle, and the ten vehicles are fully provided; the single character "mindfulness" (*nian*) is the gateway to all wonders. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one wishes to sever the suffering of all existence, one should contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states:

"Second, the beginningless pure essence of bodhi is precisely that which remains when the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is separated from its conditions. These refer to the next two phrases [of the verse].
That which removes delusive defilements and confused emotions is called frost and dew; that which is the true reality (*dharmatā*) is called the bright sun of wisdom.
As the bright sun dissolves the frost and dew, so does wondrous wisdom illuminate all transgressions. Frost cannot fail to be dissolved, and transgressions cannot fail to be extinguished.
The exhortation at the conclusion of the latter half of the practice is as stated in the text.
△ The third section, the text on the circulation [of the scripture], is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; second, the conclusion by the scribe regarding the benefits.

The first part is further divided into two: first, a general explanation of the entrustment; second, a specific demonstration of the method. The first of these is further divided into three: first, the entrustment to Ānanda; second, the encouragement to practice;
third, the indication of the heterodox and the orthodox.

Having spoken these verses, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Now you should uphold this method of repentance for the six sense faculties and the visualization of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and explain it in detail for the sake of all devas and people of the world throughout the ten directions."
First, Ānanda was the upholder of the Dharma; his power of faith and compliance was profound, such that the waters of the True Dharma could be poured forth through him.
It was entrusted to you to propagate it to future generations for those who uphold this repentance—this is the entrustment of its great function.

The contemplation of the Dharma of Samantabhadra is the entrustment of its essential principle (*tattva*). The supernatural powers of the *Lotus Sūtra* which consolidate the essentials and ensure its circulation are all examples of this.
△ Next, the exhortation to practice consists of four parts; first is the exhortation to abandon clamor and bustle.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples should uphold, read, recite, or explain the Vaipulya sūtras, they should dwell in a quiet place—whether among burial mounds, beneath forest trees, or in a forest hermitage (araṇya).
Now, for one who enters the Way, the dwelling must be quiet; the bustling markets of cities are not suitable.

There are twelve types of *dhūta* practices, of which three locations are now mentioned. First is the *āraṇya*, here translated as a "secluded and tranquil place," which refers to a remote and open area where even the sound of a single cowherd or a single drum can be heard;
in such places, one may practice meditation, which brings ten benefits, as detailed elsewhere.
The concise explanation of the method for contemplation is as described above (etc.).
Regarding "the power of mindfulness and so forth," this next section raises the exhortation to see the Buddha:

by reading and reciting the Vaipulya sutras and contemplating the meaning of the Mahāyāna, one’s power of mindfulness becomes strong; therefore, one attains the vision of my body and that of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
The stupas [contain] the infinite Buddhas who are emanations throughout the ten directions.
Those who are strong discern that this is no weakling; there must be extraordinary merit to meet an extraordinary person.
The signs seen are as extensively described above.
△ Third, the exhortation to receive offerings:

The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, out of reverence for the Dharma, held various exquisite flowers and stood in mid-air to praise and pay homage to those who practice and uphold this Dharma; one need only recite [the following].
Because this is a Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas offer worship day and night to those who uphold this Dharma.
Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode); his name signifies that his enlightened nature is clear and distinct, and he eternally delights in its manifest brilliance.
As for Bhaiṣajyarāja, he attained patience by burning his own body and has widely propagated this wondrous teaching; now is precisely the time when they both hold the flower of the single reality.

Although one who dwells in the space of the *sambhogakāya* (寂光) praises and honors the practitioner to lead in the novices, this is primarily because the practitioner’s debt to the grace of the Dharma is profound;
as for receiving offerings in return, it is because the Dharma upheld by the practitioner is the Teacher of the Buddhas,
and thus even the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, though called the "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), is himself supplied with offerings.
△ Fourth, the exhortation on the eradication of offenses:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Because I and the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, as well as the Buddhas of the ten directions,
contemplated the true meaning of the Mahāyāna, we eliminated the offenses of birth and death numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
Because this is the supreme and wondrous method of repentance, one shall now attain Buddhahood in each of the ten directions.
If you wish to swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or if you wish to manifest in person before the Buddhas of the ten directions and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,

Recite Mahāyāna sūtras and contemplate the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Through the powerful and fierce force of these three methods of repentance, even transgressions that reside within the *parināmika* (transformed) state become like flowers in the sky;

thus, the offenses of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are extinguished by a single repentance, and the Buddhas of the ten directions entrust the merit of their teachings to this final stage.
The conclusion of the exhortation for those who wish to achieve [enlightenment] swiftly summarizes the preceding "Exhortation on Leading Practice.

The conclusion of the exhortation for those who wish to manifest their bodies in this world summarizes the preceding "Exhortation on Indicating the Place. △ Third, showing the false and the correct.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who wish to contemplate Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, they should perform this contemplation.
Those who perform this contemplation are said to practice the correct contemplation; any other contemplation is called a false contemplation."
Right contemplation is called the Middle Way; emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are all correctly employed.

Contemplating Samantabhadra as not being a phenomenon external to the mind—wherein the mind is Samantabhadra and the mind creates Samantabhadra, such that subject and object are utterly extinguished—is called right contemplation.

2. Śākyamuni’s single transformation is the primary master of this practice gate (*caryāmukha*). 3. This sutra is connected with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its exhortation to resolve;

both discuss practice and vows with great emphasis. Question: The sutra says that one shall behold Samantabhadra. I do not know whether this sutra has circulated in this country in the past. [End of Text]
When people saw him, they did not respond; the Bodhisattva, however, possesses both hidden and manifest responses. As for the manifest response, it is as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
there was a bhikṣu named Mahāla who once resided in a cave reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He beheld a person of golden radiance riding a white elephant, joining his palms in worship. The bhikṣu himself identified this figure as Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, when Master Nanyue was reciting the sutras, he received the touch of Samantabhadra’s hand upon his head, and a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emerged.

Also, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, when Chan Master Daqian was practicing repentance before the Fantian Pagoda in Qiantang, Samantabhadra appeared riding an elephant with its trunk hanging down to the ground.
These manifestations indeed pervade the ten directions; let us cite these three instances as evidence.
If one's response to the darkness is such that it accords with Samantabhadra’s own words— namely, "Even if this person does not see me because of their karmic obstacles,
I shall place my hand upon their head in the midst of the gloom"— then one knows that this person’s merit and benefit in protecting all living beings is inconceivable.

First, a general explanation of the benefits, which possesses the merit of extinguishing evil and generating good. Second, from "If they are śrāvakas," the specific explanation of the methods of repentance, distinguishing between those who have left the household life and those who remain at home.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who practice repentance in accordance with the Buddha’s words should know that such persons perform the practices of Samantabhadra.
Those who perform the practices of Samantabhadra do not perceive evil signs or the retribution for evil karma.

If there are sentient beings who, during the six periods of day and night, pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and contemplate the ultimate truth of profound emptiness—
By reciting the Dharma for the duration of a single finger-snap, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The first section has two parts: first, the extinction of evil causes; second, the extinction of evil effects. Regarding the extinction of causes, it says:

"The 'characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa*) signify the karma that leads to falling into undesirable states; once these evil causes of retribution are transformed, one no longer undergoes the suffering of karmic fruition."
The characteristics of karma are as explained in the *Zhiguan yecheng jing* (Treatise on the Objects of Karma in Calming and Contemplation), etc. Next, regarding the extinction of evil fruits:

by means of the profound wisdom of emptiness that penetrates to the very bottom of the true reality (*dharmatā*), one realizes that cultivated evil is identical to its nature, and understands that the substance of defilement is fundamentally void. The metaphor of a finger-snap is not in vain;

it is like a single lamp dispelling a thousand years of darkness, or a spark from a bean-sized firewood burning a log a thousand feet long. Borrowing this [metaphor], [one realizes the power of the Dharma].
When the near serves as an analogy for the distant, who would not believe it?

△ Next, regarding the passage "If one wishes to quickly achieve [enlightenment]," etc., this specifically clarifies the cultivation of goodness; "goodness" here refers to the precepts (*śīla*). There are two types of precepts:

One who practices this path is truly a child of the Buddha, born from all Buddhas; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions serve as their preceptors.

What is called the Bodhisattva precepts? They consist of the ten grave prohibitions, the forty-eight light offenses, the eighty thousand rules of majestic deportment, and so forth.

"Not requiring *karmavācanā*" means not depending on external conditions. "Receiving offerings" means that because the person who upholds the precepts possesses profound and heavy merit and virtue, they receive offerings.
One who does so brings about blessings that exceed those of making offerings to the Buddha; thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra encourages one to eat three *liang* of gold daily.
However, if the root of one's precepts is impure, the Buddha has clearly rebuked such a person, stating they may not receive offerings or benefits, even as small as a mustard seed.

Furthermore, the Ratnarāśi Sūtra states that for a bhikṣu who breaks the precepts, there is not even a place on the great earth where he may cough or spit. Students who read these accounts should take them to heart.
Self-reflection.

Regarding the necessity of restraint, the Dharma of the precepts must be treated with respect and cannot be undertaken with a frivolous mind. A treatise states:

"If the substance of the mind is frivolous, it is ethically indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and does not give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Furthermore, if one does not cultivate the intention to uphold the precepts, one will not obtain them.

However, if one creates the distant conditions for possessing the precepts in a future life, there is nothing that is not possible. Observing those currently acting as masters of the transmission of the precepts...

If one’s own precepts are incomplete, how much more so when a mind seeking gain stands before them? They are utterly bewildered by the words of the *karmavācanā* and have little knowledge of the gravity of the various regulations.

yet they act as teachers for others to receive the precepts. If those who receive the precepts from such a person commit an offense, and having committed it, receive the precepts again—[the validity of their ordination remains in doubt].
One must perform repentance; yet, having seen auspicious signs, they permit the reception of increased precepts.

As we gradually distance ourselves from the Sages, the relationship between teacher and disciple becomes confused and muddled, their conduct resembling mere child’s play. Alas! The Dharma of the Precepts has degenerated to such an extent.
I address future students: you must revere the True Dharma. Therefore, the present text contains the words: "Even if one falls into hell, do not slander the Buddha."
This is because the precepts and wisdom are most venerable and supreme.
△ Next is the method for the Three Refuges. As it says:

Having received the six grave precepts, one should next diligently cultivate unimpeded pure conduct, develop a mind of vast salvation, and receive the eight grave precepts.
Regarding the first part of the three sections of the text: both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles consist of the Three Refuges;
however, those who understand the principle and essence of the Three Refuges—which is *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena)—are few. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"If an Arhat does not know that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding, the precepts they observe are likewise not fully complete. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states: "If one does not know [the Three Jewels] as eternal..."
All forms of taking refuge as they currently exist fail to achieve fulfillment; therefore, the present sutra is called "Sublime Meaning" (Miaoyi), the purport of which lies herein.
Although the Three Jewels are one essence, the names for that essence are profoundly deep. Refuge must proceed from the fruit, and the name of the fruit is "Sublime Meaning.
Cause and effect are non-dual. My present taking of refuge—refuge means returning to the source, and reliance means leaning upon support—is the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The wondrous precepts arise from this point. Next, the six grave dharmas refer to the *upāsaka* (lay follower) precepts; that is to say:

not killing, not stealing, not claiming to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking of the faults of the assembly, and not selling intoxicants.
The *Śīlasūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas are of two kinds: first, householders; second, renunciants. The six grave [precepts] for householders are set forth here.

Regarding the "Eight Grave [Offenses]" mentioned in the *Śīla-sūtra*, among these eight grave precepts, only four apply to those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*), while the first four do not;
