The Bodhisattva-bhūmi is the fifth grave offense. If those who are impoverished or ill come to beg for alms, and one does not give them money or goods;
or if those who seek the Dharma are not given even a single verse—this is the sixth grave offense.
If, out of anger, one inflicts harm, whether by striking with the hand, or with a staff, or with a stone, harboring such hatred and resentment in one's heart—this is the seventh.

Regarding the eighth grave precept: if there are fellow teachers or fellow students who slander the Bodhisattva’s Vaipulya Dharma-treasury, yet receive, study, and uphold similar teachings that are not the true Dharma, one should not dwell with them.
If one knows for certain this, one must not praise their virtues before others.
This Bodhisattva’s eighth grave precept is explained extensively in the scriptural texts on the Bodhisattva Precepts. (Thus it is said:)
Having thus made the vow, he dedicates the merit.
Once these vows have been established, he burns various famous incenses and scatters flowers as offerings to all Buddhas in a secluded place.
Furthermore, when in the presence of various Bodhisattvas and the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one makes this declaration: "Today I have resolved to attain Bodhicitta;

by this merit, may I universally deliver all beings. Having spoken these words, one again prostrates to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and contemplates the meaning of the Vaipulya for one day, up to seven days, whether one is a monastic or a layperson.

Without requiring a preceptor, without relying on various teachers, and without the formal procedure of *jñapti-karman*, by the power of upholding and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras and through the encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to set forth in practice, one becomes the true eye of the Dharma for all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this Dharma, one naturally accomplishes the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*): precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas arise from this Dharma, receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) within the Mahāyāna sūtras.

This passage consists of four parts: first, making offerings to the Buddha to repay his kindness; second, generating the resolve to deliver sentient beings; third, universally prostrating to further progress;

and fourth, the fourfold division that completes the section. The first part is easily understood. Next, one universally supports the entire *dharmadhātu* with the goodness of the precepts and the bodhicitta.
This is the mind of perfect enlightenment. In principle, one should expound the Four Great Vows based on the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*);

while the void may come to an end, the mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings can never be exhausted. Third, regarding the three prostrations and the contemplation of the meaning up to the twenty-first day:
for the time being, one follows the period established by this present sutra to behold Samantabhadra. Fourth, as for merely receiving and upholding [the text]: the merit is attributed to its source.

The meaning of the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya) applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Now, three of these pertain to the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and the first two pertain to the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*).

"Precepts" refers to the Middle Way; "concentration" refers to the original nature and its vigorous characteristics; and "wisdom" refers to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). The latter two belong to the fruit:

"liberation" refers to the progressive severing of the burdens of afflictions, and "knowledge and vision" refers to the absence of error in discernment. Although the third [precepts] belongs to the causal stage, it is present now.
Because they are spoken of in terms of their fruit, they are all the Dharmakāya.

and śikṣamāṇās frequently violate the various precepts and rules of deportment.

"First, regarding 'śrāvakas,' this refers to those at the initial stage of the mind. If they reach the stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) or *mūrdhan* (Summit), they spontaneously develop the *samādhi-saṃvara* (concentration-precept).

From the first fruit (*srota-āpatti-phala*) onward, they necessarily develop the *mārga-saṃvara* (path-precept), and it is impossible for them to violate the complete precepts up to the *maṇi-vrata* (jewel-precept).

The eight precepts for a śrāmaṇera are: not wearing garlands, not dancing, singing, or playing music, and not sitting on high or luxurious beds; to these are added:
not handling gold, silver, or raw and wrought precious metals, and not eating past midday.

A śikṣamāṇā—translated as a "woman training in the Dharma"—is one whom the Buddha ordained to receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts and further train her mind and thoughts through six rules, because while she was a laywoman, she had been pregnant in her womb.
Because she is pregnant, one must wait until six months have passed before receiving the full Bhikṣuṇī ordination and the various codes of conduct, numbering eighty thousand such observances.
The two states of mind—craving and wrong views—are called unwholesome, evil, and demonic rākṣasas;
they would destroy even the life-preserving skin-bag [of a boat], and if one were to beg it from them, one would surely sink oneself.

It should be so. One who possesses the dharmas of a śramaṇa has the roots of precept complete and perfect. Regarding the minor confessions for the six classes of offenses, each has its own ritual procedure;
however, now, following the Mahāyāna, one practices the dharma of emptiness, wherein both mind and objects are empty, and neither offense nor non-offense can be apprehended. Thus it is.
For one who has attained thorough realization, overturning the great earth causes both grasses and trees to wither together.

As for receiving the offerings of others, its merit is attributed to the Great Teaching.

As for what is called the "Repentance Ritual for Kṣatriyas and Laymen," as for repentance, one should simply maintain a correct mind and...
Slandering the Triple Gem does not obstruct one’s renunciation, nor does it constitute an obstacle for those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya).

One should maintain mindfulness and cultivate the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti), and should also provide offerings and support to those who uphold the Mahāyāna; however, it is not strictly necessary to prostrate to them.

To practice the first repentance and the second repentance means to filially support one's parents and respectfully honor teachers and elders; this is called practicing the second repentance.
To practice the third repentance means to govern the state according to the True Dharma and not oppress the people with injustice or corruption;
this is called practicing the third repentance. To practice the fourth repentance means to issue a decree throughout all territories on the six fast days to exert [one's power]...
To cause those who come under one's influence to practice non-killing and cultivate such dharmas as these is called practicing the fourth repentance.
As for the fifth repentance, it is simply to have deep faith in cause and effect, to believe in the One True Way, and to know that the Buddha does not perish;
this is called practicing the fifth repentance.
The Sūtra states that there are five grave offenses for a Kṣatriya king that cause one to fall into the evil realms:

first, forcibly seizing the property of the Triple Gem; second, slandering the True Dharma; third, harassing and harming the disciples of the Buddha; fourth, committing the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma);

and fifth, teaching and practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action. Regarding the first [of these], not slandering the Triple Gem and so forth means to cease [evil] and cultivate the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti) and other such dharmas.
As for those who practice good deeds yet do not observe the rites, it is because they are often arrogant toward the Buddha due to the nobility of their lineage; let them be for now.
Since you speak of providing offerings, this seems like the first act of repentance: the sin of seizing property belonging to the Triple Gem.

Second is filial piety toward one’s parents—serving their countenances without opposition—and being hidden in one's virtue so as not to offend them, just as the Great Shun served his father Gu Sou while wailing to High Heaven.

This resembles the fourth [of the ten good deeds], while the fifth is the commission of the five heinous crimes. Third, regarding "governing according to the Dharma":

this means following the Way of Heaven so that rewards and punishments are invariably appropriate—pardoning even great errors and inflicting punishment without sparing even the smallest offense—thereby ensuring that the people are not wronged and are set free through broad understanding.

One who dons the robe of shame and remorse is protected and assisted by all Buddhas; before long, such a person shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To have shame means to feel shame before the holy devas of the forty stages, to feel remorse before the worthy persons of the ten levels of faith, and furthermore, to feel shame before the [first]...

First, regarding the meaning: the Celestial Being (Yitian) felt ashamed, thinking that if a person of noble and sage-like character lacked shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), they would be a person who is naked.

Now that he has entered this stage, he is one who has donned the garment of shame and remorse. Because the Dharma-body provides hidden support and his attainment of Buddhahood is imminent, it is said that it will not be long.
△ Second, the sūtra-master’s conclusion:
When these words were spoken, ten thousand devaputras attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
Maitreya Bodhisattva and other great bodhisattvas, as well as Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Regarding the purification of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*): on a small scale, it refers to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); according to the classification of the five eyes in the Mahāyāna, the Dharma-eye resides in the eighth and ninth stages (*bhūmi*) of the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
Here, it refers to entering and abiding [in the path]. While it is termed the Buddha-eye, it is also called the Dharma-eye;

furthermore, "joy" (*prīti*) also extends to the profound, reaching even to the tenth stage where one attains the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). By practicing this for oneself and transforming others through the Dharma, all return to the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
